docs.title: 4. Arrays
docs.text: The scripts for this chapter are located in the [tableaux] folder of the project.

docs.title: 4.1. script [tab-01]
docs.text:
The following script illustrates an essential feature of TypeScript/JavaScript arrays: they are objects manipulated by reference (via pointers), not data that is copied with each assignment.

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  //: An array is an object accessed via its address
  4  const tab1: number[] = [1, 2, 3];
  5  // copying addresses
  6  const tab2: number[] = tab1;
  7  // tab1 and tab2 point to the same array
  8  console.log("tab1===tab2 :", tab1 === tab2);
  9  // You can modify the array using either tab1 or tab2
 10  tab2[1] = 10;
 11  console.log("tab1=", tab1);
 12  console.log("tab2=", tab2);

npx tsx tableaux/tab-01.ts

Execution result:

  1  tab1===tab2 : true
  2  tab1= [ 1, 10, 3 ]
  3  tab2= [ 1, 10, 3 ]
  • tab1===tab2 is true: both variables point to the same array in memory;
  • so modifying the array via tab2 also modifies what is seen through tab1—this is a direct consequence of the fact that tab1 and tab2 refer to the same data.

docs.title: 4.2. script [tab-02]
docs.text:
This script shows that the array TypeScript does not have a fixed size and behaves more like a dynamic indexed list than a traditional compiled-language array:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // array
  4  // [any] because this array will contain gaps and values of different types
  5  const tab: any[] = [];
  6  console.log("tab=", tab, ", longueur=[", tab.length, "]");
  7  console.log("-------------------------------");
  8  // initializing an element
  9  tab[3] = 100;
 10  tab[1] = "huit";
 11  // array
 12  console.log("tab=", tab, ", longueur=[", tab.length, "]");
 13  console.log("-------------------------------");
 14  // toString
 15  console.log("tab.toString=[", tab.toString(), "]");
 16  console.log("-------------------------------");
 17  // The keys of the array are its indices
 18  for (let key of tab.keys()) {
 19    console.log("clé=[", key, "], valeur=[", tab[key], "]");
 20  }
 21  console.log("-------------------------------");
 22  // the values of the array
 23  for (let value of tab.values()) {
 24    console.log("valeur=[", value, "]");
 25  }
  • line 5: const tab: any[] = [] — an empty array, typed as any[] because it will intentionally contain “gaps”;
  • lines 9–10: element #3 can be initialized even if elements 0, 1, and 2 do not yet exist—they become “gaps” (empty items), which are distinct from <span style="color: #9a3412">undefined even though they are often displayed similarly;
  • lines 15–17: the keys() and values() methods return iterators that can be traversed using for...of.
npx tsx tableaux/tab-02.ts

Execution result:

  1  tab= [] , longueur=[ 0 ]
  2  -------------------------------
  3  tab= [ <1 empty item>, 'huit', <1 empty item>, 100 ] , longueur=[ 4 ]
  4  -------------------------------
  5  tab.toString=[ ,huit,,100 ]
  6  -------------------------------
  7  clé=[ 0 ], valeur=[ undefined ]
  8  clé=[ 1 ], valeur=[ huit ]
  9  clé=[ 2 ], valeur=[ undefined ]
 10  clé=[ 3 ], valeur=[ 100 ]
 11  -------------------------------

 13  valeur=[ huit ]

docs.title: 4.3. script [tab-03]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates the main methods for manipulating an array: iterating through, adding, and removing elements.

  1  'use strict';
  2  // An array can contain different data types
  3  // [any] because this array intentionally mixes several types (demonstration)
  4  const tab: any[] = [1, 2, "un", "deux", true, [10, 20], { prop1: 10, prop2: "abc" }];
  5  // console.log can display the contents of an array
  6  show(1);
  7  console.log("tab=", tab);
  8  show(2);
  9  // Iterating through the array using `foreach`
 10  tab.forEach(element => {
 11    console.log("élément=", element, typeof (element));
 12  });
 13  show("2b");
 14  // Another way to do the same thing
 15  tab.forEach(function (element) {
 16    console.log("élément=", element, typeof (element));
 17  });
 18  show(3);
 19  // Iterating through an array using a for loop
 20  for (let i = 0; i < tab.length; i++) {
 21    console.log("i=", i, "tab[i]=", tab[i]);
 22  }
 23  show(4);
 24  // modifying tab[i]
 25  tab[5] = [];
 26  // display
 27  console.log("tab=", tab);
 28  show(5);
 29  // removing the last element from the array
 30  let element = tab.pop();
 31  console.log("élément=", element, "tab=", tab);
 32  show(6);
 33  // Add an element to the end of the array
 34  tab.push('xyz');
 35  console.log("tab=", tab);
 36  show(7);
 37  // add an element to the beginning of the array
 38  tab.unshift(1000);
 39  console.log("tab=", tab);
 40  show(8);
 41  // remove the first element
 42  element = tab.shift();
 43  console.log("élément=", element, "tab=", tab);
 44  show(9);
 45  // Removes element #2 from the array
 46  element = tab.splice(2, 1);
 47  console.log("élément=", element, "tab=", tab);
 48  show(10);
 49  // Removes two elements from the array, starting with the first element
 50  element = tab.splice(1, 2);
 51  console.log("élément=", element, "tab=", tab);
 52  
 53  // function
 54  function show(param: number | string): void {
 55    console.log("[", param, ":::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: ]");
 56  }
  • Line 4: Although tab is declared as const, its contents can be modified (line 25, <span style="color: #9a3412">tab[5] = []</span>). It is the pointer to the array that is constant, not the array itself;
  • lines 10–12: <span style="color: #9a3412">forEach iterates through the array and calls the function passed as a parameter for each element—here written using arrow notation: <span style="color: #9a3412">element => { ... }</span>;
  • lines 15–17: the same thing, written using traditional function syntax—the two forms are equivalent;
  • The methods pop(), push(), unshift(), shift(), and splice() modify the array in place (they have side effects): this is an important difference from the “immutable” methods seen in script tab-05.

docs.title: 4.4. script [tab-04]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates the functional methods for transforming an array: map, reduce, filter, find, findIndex, indexOf, sort.

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // array manipulation method
  4  
  5  // an array
  6  const tab: number[] = [];
  7  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  8    tab[i] = i * 10;
  9  }
 10  // display
 11  console.log("tab=", tab);
 12  // map
 13  const tab2 = tab.map(element => {
 14    return { prop1: element, prop2: element * element }
 15  });
 16  // display
 17  console.log("tab=", tab);
 18  console.log("tab2=", tab2);
 19  // reduce without an initial value
 20  const somme = tab.reduce((accumulator, currentValue) => accumulator + currentValue);
 21  console.log("somme tab=", somme);
 22  // reduce with initial value 10
 23  const somme2 = tab.reduce((accumulator, currentValue) => accumulator + currentValue, 10);
 24  console.log("somme2 tab=", somme2);
 25  // filter
 26  const tab4 = tab.filter((element) => {
 27    if (element > 50) {
 28      return element;
 29    }
 30  });
 31  console.log("tab4=", tab4);
 32  // find
 33  const element1 = tab.find((element) => (element > 20));
 34  console.log("élément1=", element1);
 35  // findIndex
 36  const index1 = tab.findIndex((element) => (element === 20));
 37  console.log("index1 20=", index1);
 38  // indexOf
 39  const index2 = tab.indexOf(30);
 40  console.log("index2 30=", index2);
 41  const index3 = tab.indexOf(31);
 42  console.log("index3 31=", index3);
 43  // lastIndexOf
 44  const index4 = [4, 5, 4, 2].lastIndexOf(4);
 45  console.log("index4 4=", index4);
 46  // sort
 47  const tab5 = [4, 5, 4, 2].sort();
 48  console.log("tab5=", tab5);
 49  // reverse sort
 50  const tab6 = [4, 5, 4, 2].sort((e1, e2) => {
 51    if (e1 > e2) {
 52      return -1;
 53    }
 54    else if (e1 === e2) {
 55      return 0;
 56    } else {
 57      return +1;
 58    }
 59  });
 60  console.log("tab6=", tab6);
  • [map] transforms each element and returns a new array—the original remains unchanged;
  • [reduce] “accumulates” the elements one by one into a single result. The first parameter of its function (accumulator) is the result accumulated so far; the second (currentValue) is the current element. Without an initial value (line 20), the accumulator starts with the first element of the array;
  • [filter] retains only the elements for which the function returns a “true” value;
  • [find] returns the first element that satisfies the criterion (or <span style="color: #9a3412">undefined</span>), while [findIndex] returns its index (or <span style="color: #9a3412">-1);
  • [sort] without parameters sorts in natural order. With a comparison function (e1, e2) => ..., you have complete control over the order: -1 if e1 must come before e2, +1 otherwise, 0 in case of equality.

docs.title: 4.5. script [tab-05]
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] This script presents the new array methods introduced between 2022 and 2023:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] new array methods
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7  // 1) at(index)  (ECMAScript 2022)
  8  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  9  // Previously, to access the last element of an array, we wrote tab[tab.length - 1]
 10  const tab: number[] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
 11  console.log("tab[tab.length - 1] =", tab[tab.length - 1]); // old way
 12  console.log("tab.at(-1) =", tab.at(-1)); // -> last element, more readable
 13  console.log("tab.at(-2) =", tab.at(-2)); // -> second-to-last element
 14  console.log("tab.at(0)  =", tab.at(0));  // -> equivalent to tab[0]
 15  // .at also works on strings
 16  console.log("'bonjour'.at(-1) =", "bonjour".at(-1));
 17  
 18  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 19  // 2) findLast() and findLastIndex()  (ECMAScript 2023)
 20  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 21  // symmetrical to find() / findIndex(), but starting from the end of the array
 22  const nombres: number[] = [5, 12, 8, 21, 3, 17];
 23  const dernierPair = nombres.findLast(n => n % 2 === 0);
 24  console.log("dernier nombre pair =", dernierPair); // -> 8 (the last even number counting from the end)
 25  const indexDernierPair = nombres.findLastIndex(n => n % 2 === 0);
 26  console.log("index du dernier nombre pair =", indexDernierPair);
 27  
 28  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 29  // 3) "immutable" methods  (ECMAScript 2023)
 30  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 31  // sort(), reverse(), and splice() modify the original array (side effect) — see tab-04.js
 32  // Their "to..." equivalents return an array and leave the original intact
 33  // [(number | string)[]] because toSpliced() inserts strings into this array from the bottom up
 34  const original: (number | string)[] = [4, 5, 4, 2];
 35  
 36  // toSorted: like sort(), but without modifying the original
 37  const trié = original.toSorted();
 38  console.log("original =", original, " (inchangé)");
 39  console.log("trié =", trié);
 40  
 41  // toReversed: like `reverse()`, but without modifying the original
 42  const inversé = original.toReversed();
 43  console.log("inversé =", inversé, ", original toujours =", original);
 44  
 45  // toSpliced: like `splice()`, but without modifying the original
 46  // toSpliced(indexDépart, nbÀSupprimer, ...elements to insert)
 47  const modifié: (number | string)[] = original.toSpliced(1, 2, "a", "b", "c");
 48  console.log("modifié =", modifié, ", original toujours =", original);
 49  
 50  // with(index, value): returns a copy of the array with a single element replaced
 51  const remplacé = original.with(0, 999);
 52  console.log("remplacé =", remplacé, ", original toujours =", original);
 53  
 54  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 55  // why this is useful: these methods prevent side effects, which is
 56  // particularly appreciated in front-end frameworks (React, Angular, Vue...)
 57  // where you often need to produce a new state without modifying the old one.
 58  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • [at(index)] (ES2022): secure and readable access, including with negative indices (at(-1) = last element) — more readable than tab[tab.length - 1];
  • [findLast]/[findLastIndex] (ES2023): same as find/findIndex, but starting from the end;
  • [toSorted], [toReversed], [toSpliced], [with] (ES2023): the immutable equivalents of sort, reverse, splice, and indexed assignment—they return a new array without modifying the original, unlike the methods in the tab-03 script. Very useful in front-end frameworks (React, Vue...) where you need to produce a new state without modifying the old one.
npx tsx tableaux/tab-05.ts

Execution result:

  1  tab[tab.length - 1] = 50
  2  tab.at(-1) = 50
  3  tab.at(-2) = 40
  4  tab.at(0)  = 10
  5  'bonjour'.at(-1) = r
  6  dernier nombre pair = 8
  7  index du dernier nombre pair = 2
  8  original = [ 4, 5, 4, 2 ]  (inchangé)
  9  trié = [ 2, 4, 4, 5 ]
 10  inversé = [ 2, 4, 5, 4 ] , original toujours = [ 4, 5, 4, 2 ]
 11  modifié = [ 4, 'a', 'b', 'c', 2 ] , original toujours = [ 4, 5, 4, 2 ]
 12  remplacé = [ 999, 5, 4, 2 ] , original toujours = [ 4, 5, 4, 2 ]

docs.title: 4.6. Conclusion
docs.text: The key takeaway from this chapter is that an array is an object referenced by a pointer, with no fixed size, and equipped with a rich set of methods—some of which modify the array in place (push, sort...), while others, more recent ones, consistently return a new array (toSorted, with...). The next chapter covers literal objects.

docs.title: 9. Errors and Exceptions
docs.text: TypeScript inherits the exception handling mechanism from JavaScript, which is rather basic: the [throw] statement signals an error, and the [try / catch / finally] structure catches it. The scripts in this chapter are located in the [exceptions] folder of the project.

docs.title: 9.1. script [excep-01]
docs.text:
This script displays the current time in the format hours:minutes:seconds:milliseconds using the [moment.js] library (npm install moment), then demonstrates how try/catch/finally works by triggering an error based on the parity of the current milliseconds:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // package moment
  4  import moment from 'moment';
  5  
  6  // the try/catch/finally principle
  7  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  8    // current date and time
  9    const now = Date.now();
 10    // time formatting to include milliseconds
 11    const time = moment(now).format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
 12    // milliseconds
 13    const milli = Number(time.substr(time.length - 3));
 14    // display
 15    console.log("--------------------itération n° ", i, "à", time);
 16    try {
 17      // random number
 18      const nbre = milli % 2;
 19      if (nbre === 0) {
 20        // display an error message
 21        throw "erreur";
 22      }
 23      // if you've reached this point, it means there was no error
 24      console.log("pas d'erreur");
 25    } catch (error) {
 26      // if you've reached this point, an error occurred
 27      console.log("erreur1=", error);
 28    } finally {
 29      // executed in all cases, whether there is an error or not
 30      console.log("finally")
 31    }
 32  }
  • Line 4: import moment from 'moment' — imports a third-party library, just like sprintf-js in the chapter “Strings”;
  • On each loop iteration, if the current number of milliseconds is even, an error is thrown (line 20) and caught by the <span style="color: #9a3412">catch block; otherwise, the message “no error” is displayed;
  • The [finally] clause is executed systematically, regardless of whether an error occurred or not.

This script depends on the exact execution time: the result below (obtained from an actual run) will therefore differ each time it is run—only the principle (the finally block is always executed) is guaranteed:

docs.title: 9.2. script [excep-02]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that [throw] can throw any type of data—string, array, object, or Error instance—and that this data is fully captured by the catch clause:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // You can "throw" just about anything to signal an error
  4  let i = 0;
  5  console.log("--------------------essai n° ", i);
  6  // Throw a string
  7  try {
  8    throw "msg d'erreur";
  9  } catch (error) {
 10    // an error occurred
 11    console.log("erreur=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
 12  }
 13  // Throw a literal object
 14  i++;
 15  console.log("--------------------essai n° ", i);
 16  try {
 17    throw [1, 2, 3]
 18  } catch (error) {
 19    // An error occurred
 20    console.log("erreur=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
 21  }
 22  // Throw an object
 23  i++;
 24  console.log("--------------------essai n° ", i);
 25  try {
 26    throw { nom: "hercule", pays: "grèce antique" }
 27  } catch (error) {
 28    // An error occurred
 29    console.log("erreur=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
 30  }
 31  // Throw an Error type
 32  i++;

[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] This script introduces two important additions introduced with ECMAScript 2022: the [cause] error option and custom error classes.

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] the [cause] property of an error  (ECMAScript 2022)
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // It is common to encounter a technical (low-level) error and to
  7  // trigger it again in the form of a more explicit (high-level) error, so that
  8  // so that the calling code better understands the business context.
  9  // AVANT In 2022, doing this caused us to lose track of the original error.
 10  
 11  function lireConfiguration(): void {
 12    // simulates a low-level technical error (e.g., file not found)
 13    throw new Error("ENOENT: fichier 'config.json' introuvable");
 14  }
 15  
 16  function démarrerApplication(): void {
 17    try {
 18      lireConfiguration();
 19    } catch (erreurTechnique) {
 20      // The second parameter {cause} allows you to link the original error
 21      // to the new error without losing the information
 22      throw new Error("impossible de démarrer l'application", { cause: erreurTechnique });
 23    }
 24  }
 25  
 26  try {
 27    démarrerApplication();
 28  } catch (erreur: any) {
 29    console.log("erreur=", erreur.message);

 35  // custom error classes (available since ECMAScript 2015,
 36  // but very often used with [cause] since 2022, so reviewed here)
 37  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------

 39  // to distinguish them using [instanceof], as with ReferenceError or RangeError

 42  
 43    champEnErreur: string;

 46      // the message and the [options] (including any cause) are forwarded to the parent [Error]
 47      super(message, options);
 48      // The default name would be "Error"; it can be customized
 49      this.name = "ErreurValidation";
 50      // Business-specific information for this type of error can be added
 51      this.champEnErreur = champEnErreur;
 52    }
 53  }

 56    if (typeof (âge) !== "number") {

 58    }

 61    }

 63  }

 70    } catch (erreur) {

 77      }
 78    }

docs.title: 11. Event-Driven Programming and Asynchronous Functions
docs.text:
An asynchronous function is a function whose execution is initiated but whose result is not immediately awaited. When execution is complete, the asynchronous function signals its result—via an event, or via a [Promise], as we will see later.

This mode of operation is well-suited for execution in a browser, where the application constantly responds to events (clicks, keystrokes, network responses, etc.). The scripts in this chapter are executed by [node.js], which also uses an event loop:

  • execution of the script’s main code is the first event processed;
  • if this code has initiated asynchronous tasks, script execution continues until they are complete—they emit an event once finished, which is queued in the event loop;
  • the main script must subscribe to these events to retrieve their results;
  • the script does not terminate until all the events it has emitted have been processed.

The scripts in this chapter are located in the [async] folder of the project.

docs.title: 11.1. script [async-01]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates the behavior of a script containing an asynchronous action, using the native function [setTimeout]:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // imports
  4  import moment from 'moment';
  5  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  6  
  7  // start
  8  const débutScript = moment(Date.now());
  9  console.log("[début du script],", heure());
 10  
 11  // setTimeout sets a 1000-ms timer (second parameter) and immediately returns the timer ID
 12  // When the timer has elapsed for 1000 ms, it emits an event that is queued by the runtime
 13  // When the event is processed by the runtime, the function (first parameter) is executed
 14  setTimeout(function () {
 15    // This code will be executed when the timer reaches 0
 16    console.log("[fin de l'action asynchrone setTimeout],", heure(débutScript));
 17  }, 1000)
 18  
 19  // will be displayed before the message from the timer’s internal function
 20  console.log("[fin du code principal du script],", heure(débutScript));
 21  
 22  // utility for displaying time and duration
 23  function heure(début?: moment.Moment): string {
 24    // current time
 25    const now = moment(Date.now());
 26    // time formatting
 27    let result = "heure=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
 28    // Should a duration be calculated?
 29    if (début) {
 30      const durée = now.valueOf() - début.valueOf();
 31      const milliseconds = durée % 1000;
 32      const seconds = Math.floor(durée / 1000);
 33      // time and duration formatting
 34      result = result + sprintf(", durée= %s seconde(s) et %s millisecondes", seconds, milliseconds);
 35    }
 36    // result
 37    return result;
 38  }
  • Lines 14–17: [setTimeout] takes two parameters: a function to execute and a delay in milliseconds. It executes instantly: it starts a timer and immediately returns control, without waiting for the delay to expire;
  • line 19: this message is therefore displayed before the one on line 15, even though it is written later in the code;
  • line 22: function heure(start?: moment.Moment): string — the start parameter is optional (?), of type moment.Moment; if provided, the function calculates and adds the elapsed time.
npx tsx async/async-01.ts

Execution result:

  1  [début du script], heure=07:41:36:456
  2  [fin du code principal du script], heure=07:41:36:457, durée= 0 seconde(s) et 2 millisecondes
  3  [fin de l'action asynchrone setTimeout], heure=07:41:37:458, durée= 1 seconde(s) et 3 millisecondes

We can see that the asynchronous action setTimeout completes about 1 second after the main code finishes—which is exactly the programmed delay. The overall script, however, does not complete until this asynchronous task is finished.

Note: We’ll use setTimeout to simulate asynchronous tasks throughout this chapter. A real asynchronous task (network request, file read, etc.) behaves in the same way: it yields control immediately and then reports its result later—usually via two possible events, one for success and one for failure.

docs.title: 11.2. script [async-02]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates how an asynchronous function can communicate its result by emitting events, using the native class EventEmitter (node:events module):

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // Asynchronous functions can return a result by emitting an event
  4  // The main code can retrieve these results by subscribing to the emitted events
  5  
  6  // imports
  7  import moment from 'moment';
  8  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  9  import EventEmitter from 'events';
 10  
 11  // start
 12  const débutScript = moment(Date.now());
 13  console.log("[début du script],", heure());
 14  // an event emitter
 15  const eventEmitter = new EventEmitter();
 16  
 17  // setTimeout sets a 1000 ms timer (2nd parameter) and immediately returns the timer ID
 18  // When the timer has elapsed for 1000 ms, it emits an event that is queued by the runtime
 19  // When the event is processed by the runtime, the function (first parameter) is executed
 20  setTimeout(function () {
 21    // This code will be executed when the timer reaches 0
 22    console.log("[setTimeout, fin du timer d'1 s],", heure(débutScript));
 23    // An event is triggered to indicate that a result is available
 24    eventEmitter.emit("timer1Success", { success: 4 });
 25    // Another event is triggered to indicate that another result is available
 26    eventEmitter.emit("timer1Failure", { failure: 6 });
 27  }, 1000)
 28  
 29  // Subscribe to the event [timer1Success]
 30  eventEmitter.on('timer1Success', (result) => {
 31    console.log(sprintf("la fonction asynchrone du timer a rendu le résultat [%j], %s, via l'événement [timer1Success]", result, heure(débutScript)));
 32  });
 33  
 34  // Subscribe to the event [timer1Failure]
 35  eventEmitter.on('timer1Failure', (result) => {
 36    console.log(sprintf("la fonction asynchrone du timer a rendu le résultat [%j], %s, via l'événement [timer1Failure]", result, heure(débutScript)));
 37  });
 38  
 39  // will be displayed before the event messages sent by the function associated with [timer1]
 40  console.log("[fin du code principal du script],", heure(débutScript));
 41  
 42  // utility for displaying time and duration
 43  function heure(début?: moment.Moment): string {
 44    // current time
 45    const now = moment(Date.now());
 46    // time formatting
 47    let result = "heure=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
 48    // Should a duration be calculated?
 49    if (début) {
 50      const durée = now.valueOf() - début.valueOf();
 51      const milliseconds = durée % 1000;
 52      const seconds = Math.floor(durée / 1000);
 53      // time and duration formatting
 54      result = result + sprintf(", durée= %s seconde(s) et %s millisecondes", seconds, milliseconds);
 55    }
 56    // result
 57    return result;
 58  }
  • Line 8: import EventEmitter from 'events' — imports the class that allows you to trigger and listen for events;
  • line 15: const eventEmitter = new EventEmitter() — an event emitter is instantiated using <span style="color: #9a3412">new;
  • lines 24 and 26: the function encapsulated in setTimeout emits two events, timer1Success and timer1Failure, each with its own associated data (here, for demonstration purposes only—normally, a single task would emit only one or the other);
  • lines 29–37: the main code subscribes to these two events using eventEmitter.on(nomÉvénement, callback)—the callback will not execute until the event is actually emitted, not at the time of subscription;
  • line 40: the main code ends here, but the global script does not end until the asynchronous task (and the subscribed callbacks) have finished executing.

  2  [fin du code principal du script], heure=07:41:38:170, durée= 0 seconde(s) et 7 millisecondes
  3  [setTimeout, fin du timer d'1 s], heure=07:41:39:173, durée= 1 seconde(s) et 10 millisecondes

docs.title: 11.4. The Promise Mechanism
docs.text:
The type [Promise] is a class that avoids explicitly managing events: this is done implicitly, but understanding the underlying events helps provide a better grasp of how it works. Its constructor takes an asynchronous function as a parameter, to which it passes two functions, traditionally named [resolve] and [reject]:

const promise = new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
   // an asynchronous task is launched
  // ...
   // if successful: call resolve(result), where [result] is the result of the task
   // if failure: call reject(error), where [error] encapsulates the error encountered
});

A Promise object can be in one of four states:

  • [pending]: the asynchronous task is not yet complete;
  • [fulfilled]: it has completed successfully;
  • [rejected]: it has failed;
  • [settled]: it has completed (regardless of whether it succeeded or failed).

You subscribe to the results of a Promise using the syntax promise.then(f1).catch(f2).finally(f3): f1 executes on success (it receives the result passed by resolve), f2 on failure (it receives the error passed by <span style="color: #9a3412">reject), and f3 in all cases, without any parameters.

docs.title: 11.5. script [async-04]
docs.text:
This script creates two independent Promises, each encapsulating a setTimeout, and subscribes to their results:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // It is possible to obtain the results (success, failure) of an asynchronous function
  4  // without explicitly using events, thanks to the [Promise] class
  5  // This class implicitly uses events, but they are not visible in the code
  6  
  7  // imports
  8  import moment from 'moment';
  9  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
 10  
 11  // start
 12  const débutScript = moment(Date.now());
 13  console.log("[début du script],", heure(débutScript));
 14  
 15  // Definition of an asynchronous task using a promise [Promise]
 16  // The asynchronous task is the constructor parameter [Promise]
 17  const débutPromise1 = moment(Date.now());
 18  const promise1 = new Promise<string>(function (resolve) {
 19    // log
 20    console.log("[début fonction asynchrone de promise1],", heure(débutPromise1));
 21    // asynchronous code
 22    setTimeout(function () {
 23      // This code is executed after a 1-second delay (second parameter)
 24      console.log("[fin fonction asynchrone de promise1],", heure(débutPromise1));
 25      // the asynchronous task returns a result using the function [resolve]
 26      // The promise is then fulfilled
 27      resolve('[réussite]');
 28    }, 1000)
 29  });

 32  // once the promise has been resolved or rejected
 33  // The following statement is a subscription to the event [resolved] via the method [then]
 34  // and to event [rejected] via method [catch]
 35  // the [finally] method is executed whether after a "then" or a "catch"
 36  promise1.then(result => {
 37    // if the promise succeeds  [evt resolved]
 38    console.log(sprintf("[promise1.then], %s, result=%s", heure(débutPromise1), result));

 40    // error case  [evt rejected]
 41    console.log(sprintf("[promise1.catch], %s, result=%s", heure(débutPromise1), result));
 42  }).finally(() => {
 43    // executed in all cases
 44    console.log("[promise1.finally]", heure(débutPromise1));
 45  });

 48  const débutPromise2 = moment(Date.now());
 49  const promise2 = new Promise<string>(function (resolve, reject) {
 50    // log
 51    console.log("[début fonction asynchrone de promise2],", heure(débutPromise2));
 52    // asynchronous task
 53    setTimeout(function () {
 54      console.log("[fin fonction asynchrone de promise2],", heure(débutPromise2));
 55      // The asynchronous task returns a result using the function [reject]
 56      // The promise then fails
 57      reject('[échec]');
 58    }, 2000)
 59  });
 60

 62  // once it has been resolved or rejected

 64    // if the promise succeeds [evt resolved]
 65    console.log(sprintf("[promise2.then], %s, result=%s", heure(débutPromise2), result));
 66  }).catch(result => {

 69  }).finally(() => {

docs.title: 11.6. script [async-05]
docs.text:
It is most common to define an asynchronous function that returns a Promise, rather than creating the Promise object directly—which is useful when the function requires parameters. This script defines two asynchronous functions and waits for both of them to complete using [Promise.all]:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // You can define asynchronous functions that return a type [Promise]
  4  // They can then be tagged with the keyword [async]
  5  // again
  6  // imports
  7  import moment from 'moment';
  8  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  9  
 10  // start
 11  const débutScript = moment(Date.now());
 12  console.log("[début du script],", heure());
 13  
 14  // format of the result returned by async01 and async02
 15  interface RésultatAsync {
 16    prop1: number[];
 17    prop2: string;
 18    prop3: number;
 19  }
 20  
 21  // an asynchronous function can return a promise [Promise]
 22  // and thus have the attribute [async]
 23  async function async01(p1: number): Promise<RésultatAsync> {
 24    return new Promise<RésultatAsync>(resolve => {
 25      console.log("[début de la tâche asynchrone async01]");
 26      // the asynchronous task
 27      const débutAsync01 = moment(Date.now());
 28      setTimeout(function () {
 29        // This code is executed after a 1-second delay (second parameter)
 30        console.log("[fin de la tâche asynchrone async01],", heure(débutAsync01));
 31        // the asynchronous task can return a complex result
 32        resolve({
 33          prop1: [10, 20, 30],
 34          prop2: "abcd",
 35          prop3: p1,
 36        });
 37      }, 1000)
 38    });
 39  }
 40  
 41  // A function can return a promise [Promise]
 42  // and may then have the attribute [async]
 43  async function async02(p1: number, p2: number): Promise<RésultatAsync> {
 44    return new Promise<RésultatAsync>(resolve => {
 45      console.log("[début de la tâche asynchrone async02]");
 46      // asynchronous task
 47      const débutAsync02 = moment(Date.now());
 48      setTimeout(function () {
 49        // the following code is executed after a 2-second delay (second parameter)
 50        console.log("[fin de la tâche asynchrone async02],", heure(débutAsync02));
 51        // the asynchronous task may return a complex result
 52        resolve({
 53          prop1: [11, 21, 31],
 54          prop2: "xyzt",
 55          prop3: p1 + p2
 56        });
 57      }, 2000)
 58    })
 59  }
 60  
 61  // Both asynchronous functions are launched in parallel
 62  // and we wait for both of them to finish
 63  // The `then` block will only execute if both functions have emitted the event [resolved]
 64  // The `catch` block will execute as soon as either of the two functions emits the event [rejected]
 65  Promise.all([async01(10), async02(10, 20)])
 66    //. The result is an array [result1, result2], where [result1] is the result emitted by a [resolve] from [async01]
 67    //, and [result2] is the result output by a [resolve] of [async02]
 68    .then(result => {
 69      console.log(sprintf("[promise-all success], %s, result=%j", heure(débutScript), result));
 70    })
 71    // error is the result returned by the first [reject] from one of the two asynchronous functions
 72    .catch(error => {
 73      console.log(sprintf("[promise-all error], %s, erreur=%j", heure(débutScript), error));
 74    })
 75    // "finally" is executed after "then" or "catch"
 76    .finally(() => {
 77      console.log(sprintf("[promise-all finally], %s", heure(débutScript)));
 78    });
 79  
 80  // will be displayed before the messages from the asynchronous functions and associated events
 81  console.log("[fin du code principal du script],", heure(débutScript));
 82  
 83  // utility
 84  function heure(début?: moment.Moment): string {
 85    // current time
 86    const now = moment(Date.now());
 87    // time formatting
 88    let result = "heure=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
 89    if (début) {
 90      const durée = now.valueOf() - début.valueOf();
 91      const milliseconds = durée % 1000;
 92      const seconds = Math.floor(durée / 1000);
 93      // duration formatting
 94      result = result + sprintf(", durée= %s seconde(s) et %s millisecondes", seconds, milliseconds);
 95    }
 96    // result
 97    return result;
 98  }
  • Lines 20 and 36: The asynchronous functions are typed as Promise<RésultatAsync> thanks to the RésultatAsync interface defined above;
  • line 62: [Promise.all([...])] waits for all promises in the array to resolve before executing its then—as soon as one fails, its catch executes immediately, without waiting for the others;
  • the two tasks run in parallel (their respective waits overlap): the total duration (~2s) corresponds to the longer of the two, not to their sum (~3s).

  3  [début de la tâche asynchrone async02]
  4  [fin du code principal du script], heure=07:42:32:180, durée= 0 seconde(s) et 6 millisecondes

docs.title: 11.7. [async-06] script — async / await
docs.text:
The keywords [async]/[await] allow you to write asynchronous code that looks like synchronous code: the underlying event handling is completely hidden, which makes the code much easier to read. This script defines three asynchronous functions—the third one fails intentionally—and executes them first sequentially, then in parallel:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // parallel or sequential execution of multiple asynchronous tasks
  4  // with the keywords async / await
  5  
  6  // imports
  7  import moment from 'moment';
  8  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  9  
 10  // start
 11  const débutScript = moment(Date.now());
 12  console.log("[début du code principal du script],", heure());
 13  
 14  // Format of the result returned by async01/async02/async03
 15  interface RésultatAsync {
 16    prop1: number[];
 17    prop2: string;
 18  }
 19  
 20  // an asynchronous function returning a [Promise]
 21  async function async01(débutAsync01: moment.Moment): Promise<RésultatAsync> {
 22    return new Promise(function (resolve) {
 23      console.log("[début fonction asynchrone async01],", heure());
 24      // asynchronous function
 25      setTimeout(function () {
 26        console.log("[fin fonction asynchrone async01],", heure(débutAsync01));
 27        // The asynchronous operation can return a complex result
 28        // success here
 29        resolve({
 30          prop1: [11, 21, 31],
 31          prop2: "abcd"
 32        });
 33      }, 1000)
 34    });
 35  }
 36  
 37  // an asynchronous function returning a [Promise]
 38  async function async02(débutAsync02: moment.Moment): Promise<RésultatAsync> {
 39    console.log("[début fonction asynchrone async02],", heure());
 40    return new Promise(function (resolve) {
 41      // asynchronous function
 42      setTimeout(function () {
 43        console.log("[fin fonction asynchrone async02],", heure(débutAsync02));
 44        // an asynchronous action can return a complex result
 45        // success here
 46        resolve({
 47          prop1: [12, 22, 32],
 48          prop2: "xyzt"
 49        });
 50      }, 2000)
 51    })
 52  }
 53  
 54  // an asynchronous function returning a [Promise]
 55  async function async03(débutAsync03: moment.Moment): Promise<RésultatAsync> {
 56    console.log("[début fonction asynchrone async03],", heure());
 57    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
 58      // asynchronous function
 59      setTimeout(function () {
 60        console.log("[fin fonction asynchrone async03],", heure(débutAsync03));
 61        // an asynchronous action can return a complex result
 62        // Failure here
 63        reject({
 64          prop1: [13, 23, 33],
 65          prop2: "échec"
 66        });
 67      }, 3000)
 68    })
 69  }
 70  
 71  // asynchronous function - using async/await
 72  async function main(): Promise<void> {
 73    const débutSequential = moment(Date.now());
 74    // sequential execution of asynchronous tasks
 75    console.log("------------ exécution séquentielle des tâches asynchrones lancée ------------------------")
 76    try {
 77      // Execution while waiting for [async01]
 78      const débutAsync01 = moment(Date.now());
 79      const result1 = await async01(débutAsync01);
 80      console.log("[async01 result]=", result1);
 81      // Execution with waiting for [async02]
 82      const débutAsync02 = moment(Date.now());
 83      console.log("début async02-------------", heure());
 84      const result2 = await async02(débutAsync02);
 85      console.log("[async02 result]=", result2);
 86      // Execution while waiting for [async03]
 87      const débutAsync03 = moment(Date.now());
 88      console.log("début async03-------------", heure());
 89      const result3 = await async03(débutAsync03);
 90      console.log("[async03 result]=", result3);
 91    } catch (error) {
 92      // One of the asynchronous actions failed
 93      console.log(sprintf("[sequential error]= %j, %s", error, heure(débutSequential)));
 94    } finally {
 95      // completed
 96      console.log("[fin exécution séquentielle des tâches asynchrones],", heure(débutSequential));
 97    }
 98  
 99    const débutParallel = moment(Date.now());
100    // parallel execution of asynchronous tasks
101    console.log("------------ exécution parallèle des tâches asynchrones lancée ------------------------");
102    try {
103      const result = await Promise.all([async01(débutParallel), async02(débutParallel), async03(débutParallel)]);
104      console.log(sprintf("[parallel success], %s, result=%j", heure(débutParallel), result));
105    } catch (error) {
106      // One of the asynchronous actions failed
107      console.log(sprintf("[parallel error], %s, erreur=%j", heure(débutParallel), error));
108    } finally {
109      // Completed
110      console.log(sprintf("[fin exécution parallèle des tâches asynchrones],%s", heure(débutParallel)));
111    }
112  
113    // completed
114    console.log("[fin de la fonction main],", heure(débutSequential));
115  }
116  // execution of the "main" asynchronous function
117  main();
118  
119  // will be displayed before the various messages from the asynchronous functions and their events
120  console.log("[fin du code principal du script],", heure(débutScript));
121  
122  // utility
123  function heure(début?: moment.Moment): string {
124    // current time
125    const now = moment(Date.now());
126    // time formatting
127    let result = "heure=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
128    if (début) {
129      const durée = now.valueOf() - début.valueOf();
130      const milliseconds = durée % 1000;
131      const seconds = Math.floor(durée / 1000);
132      // duration formatting
133      result = result + sprintf(", durée= %s seconde(s) et %s millisecondes", seconds, milliseconds);
134    }
135    // result
136    return result;
137  }
  • line 79: async function main(): Promise<void> — an async-tagged function always returns a Promise, even if its body does not explicitly indicate this;
  • line 87: await async01(débutAsync01) suspends the execution of main until the promise is resolved, without blocking the rest of the program (the await keyword can only be used inside an <span style="color: #9a3412">async</span> function or at the top level of a module—see the chapter “Modules,” script <span style="color: #9a3412">import-04</span>);
  • lines 85–100: sequential execution—each await waits for the previous task to finish before starting the next one; the total duration is the sum of the three wait times (~6s);
  • lines 106–113: parallel execution, with await Promise.all([...])</span>—the total duration is that of the longest task (~3s);
  • A standard try/catch block is sufficient to handle the failure of an awaited promise—there’s no longer a need for chained .catch() calls as in the previous scripts.
    • npx tsx async/async-06.ts

    Execution result:

      1  [début du code principal du script], heure=07:42:34:907
  2  ------------ exécution séquentielle des tâches asynchrones lancée ------------------------
  3  [début fonction asynchrone async01], heure=07:42:34:914
  4  [fin du code principal du script], heure=07:42:34:915, durée= 0 seconde(s) et 8 millisecondes
  5  [fin fonction asynchrone async01], heure=07:42:35:916, durée= 1 seconde(s) et 2 millisecondes
  6  [async01 result]= { prop1: [ 11, 21, 31 ], prop2: 'abcd' }
  7  début async02------------- heure=07:42:35:917
  8  [début fonction asynchrone async02], heure=07:42:35:918
  9  [fin fonction asynchrone async02], heure=07:42:37:920, durée= 2 seconde(s) et 3 millisecondes
 10  [async02 result]= { prop1: [ 12, 22, 32 ], prop2: 'xyzt' }
 11  début async03------------- heure=07:42:37:921
 12  [début fonction asynchrone async03], heure=07:42:37:921
 13  [fin fonction asynchrone async03], heure=07:42:40:925, durée= 3 seconde(s) et 4 millisecondes
 14  [sequential error]= {"prop1":[13,23,33],"prop2":"échec"}, heure=07:42:40:925, durée= 6 seconde(s) et 15 millisecondes
 15  [fin exécution séquentielle des tâches asynchrones], heure=07:42:40:925, durée= 6 seconde(s) et 15 millisecondes
 16  ------------ exécution parallèle des tâches asynchrones lancée ------------------------
 17  [début fonction asynchrone async01], heure=07:42:40:926
 18  [début fonction asynchrone async02], heure=07:42:40:926
 19  [début fonction asynchrone async03], heure=07:42:40:926
 20  [fin fonction asynchrone async01], heure=07:42:41:927, durée= 1 seconde(s) et 2 millisecondes
 21  [fin fonction asynchrone async02], heure=07:42:42:925, durée= 2 seconde(s) et 0 millisecondes
 22  [fin fonction asynchrone async03], heure=07:42:43:926, durée= 3 seconde(s) et 1 millisecondes

docs.title: 11.8. [async-07] script — Promise extensions
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] This script presents four extensions introduced between 2020 and 2024, which are now widely used in modern TypeScript:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] extensions to the Promise class
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // small utility function: returns a promise that succeeds or fails after [délai] ms
  7  function tâche(nom: string, délai: number, réussit: boolean): Promise<string> {
  8    return new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
  9      setTimeout(() => {
 10        if (réussit) {
 11          resolve(`résultat de ${nom}`);
 12        } else {
 13          reject(`échec de ${nom}`);
 14        }
 15      }, délai);
 16    });
 17  }
 18  
 19  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 20  // 1) Promise.allSettled()  (ECMAScript 2020)
 21  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 22  // async-05.js shows Promise.all(): if UNE of the promises fails, the catch is triggered
 23  // and the results of the other promises—which were successful—are lost
 24  // Promise.allSettled() waits for TOUJOURS until all promises are complete
 25  // (whether successful or failed) and returns the details of each one, without ever rejecting
 26  async function démoAllSettled(): Promise<void> {
 27    console.log("--- Promise.allSettled ---");
 28    const résultats = await Promise.allSettled([
 29      tâche("tâche1", 300, true),
 30      tâche("tâche2", 200, false),
 31      tâche("tâche3", 100, true)
 32    ]);
 33    // Each element has the form { status: "fulfilled", value: ... } or { status: "rejected", reason: ... }
 34    résultats.forEach((résultat, index) => {
 35      if (résultat.status === "fulfilled") {
 36        console.log(`tâche${index + 1} réussie :`, résultat.value);
 37      } else {
 38        console.log(`tâche${index + 1} échouée :`, résultat.reason);
 39      }
 40    });
 41  }
 42  
 43  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 44  // 2) Promise.any()  (ECMAScript 2021)
 45  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 46  // returns the result of the successful PREMIÈRE promise (the others are ignored)
 47  // fails only if the TOUTES promises fail (with a AggregateError containing the errors)
 48  async function démoAny(): Promise<void> {
 49    console.log("--- Promise.any ---");
 50    try {
 51      const résultat = await Promise.any([
 52        tâche("miroir-lent", 500, true),
 53        tâche("miroir-rapide", 100, true),
 54        tâche("miroir-en-panne", 50, false)
 55      ]);
 56      console.log("premier miroir disponible :", résultat);
 57    } catch (erreurGlobale: any) {
 58      // erreurGlobale.errors contains the list of all individual errors
 59      console.log("tous les miroirs ont échoué :", erreurGlobale.errors);
 60    }
 61  }
 62  
 63  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 64  // 3) Promise.withResolvers()  (ECMAScript 2024)
 65  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 66  // Previously, to "extract" the resolve/reject functions from the Promise constructor
 67  // (e.g., to call them much later, elsewhere in the code), you had to
 68  // a somewhat artificial intermediate variable:
 69  //   let resolveExterne;
 70  //   const promise = new Promise(resolve => { resolveExterne = resolve; });
 71  // Promise.withResolvers() does this directly, in a single expression
 72  function démoWithResolvers(): Promise<string> {
 73    console.log("--- Promise.withResolvers ---");
 74    const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers<string>();
 75  
 76    // You can resolve the promise from anywhere, for example, within another callback
 77    setTimeout(() => {
 78      console.log("[callback externe] on déclenche la résolution de la promesse");
 79      resolve("valeur transmise depuis un callback externe");
 80    }, 200);
 81  
 82    return promise;
 83  }
 84  
 85  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 86  // 4) Cancel an asynchronous operation with AbortController
 87  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 88  // AbortController allows you to cancel a pending asynchronous operation (fetch, timers, etc.)
 89  // is the standard mechanism used by [fetch] for timeouts (see http/fetch-01.js)
 90  function tâcheAnnulable(délai: number, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<string> {
 91    return new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
 92      const timer = setTimeout(() => resolve("terminé normalement"), délai);
 93      // If the cancellation signal is triggered, everything is stopped and the operation is rejected
 94      signal.addEventListener("abort", () => {
 95        clearTimeout(timer);
 96        reject(new Error("opération annulée : " + signal.reason));
 97      });
 98    });
 99  }
100  
101  async function démoAbortController(): Promise<void> {
102    console.log("--- AbortController ---");
103    const contrôleur = new AbortController();
104    // The cancellation is scheduled for 100 ms from now, before the task’s normal completion (500 ms)
105    setTimeout(() => contrôleur.abort("délai dépassé côté utilisateur"), 100);
106    try {
107      const résultat = await tâcheAnnulable(500, contrôleur.signal);
108      console.log("résultat =", résultat);
109    } catch (erreur: any) {
110      console.log("erreur :", erreur.message);
111    }
112  }
113  
114  // Execute the demonstrations sequentially
115  async function main(): Promise<void> {
116    await démoAllSettled();
117    await démoAny();
118    console.log("--- Promise.withResolvers, résultat ---", await démoWithResolvers());
119    await démoAbortController();
120  }
121  
122  main();
  • [Promise.allSettled] (ES2020): unlike Promise.all (async-05 script), it always waits for all promises to complete—whether they succeed or fail—and returns the details of each one—which is useful when you never want to lose the results of tasks that succeeded, even if another one failed;
  • [Promise.any] (ES2021): returns the result of the first promise that succeeds, ignoring the others—only rejects if all fail;
  • [Promise.withResolvers] (ES2024): extracts resolve and reject from the Promise constructor into a single expression, which is useful for resolving a promise later from another part of the code;
  • [AbortController]: allows you to cancel a pending asynchronous operation—this is the standard mechanism used by <span style="color: #9a3412">fetch</span> for timeouts (see the chapter “The HTTP Functions”).
npx tsx async/async-07.ts

Execution result:

  1  --- Promise.allSettled ---
  2  tâche1 réussie : résultat de tâche1
  3  tâche2 échouée : échec de tâche2
  4  tâche3 réussie : résultat de tâche3
  5  --- Promise.any ---
  6  premier miroir disponible : résultat de miroir-rapide
  7  --- Promise.withResolvers ---
  8  [callback externe] on déclenche la résolution de la promesse
  9  --- Promise.withResolvers, résultat --- valeur transmise depuis un callback externe
 10  --- AbortController ---
 11  erreur : opération annulée : délai dépassé côté utilisateur

This script examines how parameters are passed to a function: by value for numbers, strings, and booleans; by reference for arrays, literal objects, and functions.

  1  'use strict';
  2  // function parameter passing mode
  3  // -----------------------number - pass-by-value

docs.title: 8.2. script [func-02]
docs.text:
This script shows that [function] is a data type like any other: a variable can have this type, and there are two ways to define a function—using the <span style="color: #9a3412">function</span> keyword or the arrow notation =></span>. 

  1  'use strict';
  2  // You can assign a function to a variable
  3  const variable1: (a: number, b: number) => number = function (a, b) {
  4    return a + b;
  5  };
  6  console.log("typeof(variable1)=", typeof (variable1));
  7  // the variable can then be used as a function
  8  console.log("variable1(10,12)=", variable1(10, 12));
  9  // the function can be defined using the => notation
 10  const variable2: (a: number, b: number, c: number) => number = (a, b, c) => {
 11    return a - b + c;
 12  };
 13  console.log("variable2(10,12,14)=", variable2(10, 12, 14));
 14  // You can omit the curly braces if there is only one expression in the function body
 15  // This expression is then the function’s return value
 16  const variable3 = (a: number, b: number, c: number): number => a + b + c;
 17  console.log("variable3(10,12,14)=", variable3(10, 12, 14));
  • line 3: const variable1: (a: number, b: number) => number = function (a, b) {...} — the type of a function variable is declared as a signature (parameters) => typeDeRetour;
  • Lines 10–12: The same thing using arrow notation: (a, b, c) => { ... };
  • line 16: without curly braces, the function body is reduced to a single expression, which automatically becomes the return value — (a, b, c): number => a + b + c.

  3  variable2(10,12,14)= 12

docs.title: 8.3. script [func-03]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that a function can be passed as an argument to another function—a technique widely used in the TypeScript/JavaScript frameworks (callbacks, map/filter/reduce from the “Arrays” chapter...):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // A function's parameters can be of type [fonction]
  3  
  4  // function f1
  5  function f1(param1: number, param2: number): number {
  6    return param1 + param2 + 10;
  7  }
  8  // function f2
  9  function f2(param1: number, param2: number): number {
 10    return param1 + param2 + 20;
 11  }
 12  // function g with function f as a parameter
 13  function g(param1: number, param2: number, f: (a: number, b: number) => number): number {
 14    return f(param1, param2) + 100;
 15  }
 16  // Uses of g
 17  console.log(g(0, 10, f1));
 18  console.log(g(0, 10, f2));
 19  // the actual function-type parameter can be passed by reference—form 1
 20  console.log(g(0, 10, (param1, param2) => {
 21    return param1 + param2 + 30;
 22  }));
 23  // The actual function-type parameter can be passed by reference—form 2
 24  console.log(g(0, 10, function (param1, param2) {
 25    return param1 + param2 + 40;
 26  }));
  • line 13: function g(param1: number, param2: number, f: (a: number, b: number) => number): number — the third parameter f is itself typed as a function;
  • lines 20–22 and 24–26: the actual function-type parameter can be passed directly, either as an arrow function or a regular function, without first being stored in a variable.

docs.title: 8.4. script [func-04]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that a function can behave like a class—a mechanism that predates ES6 but is still valid, although it has now been replaced by the class keyword (see the chapter “Classes”):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // A function can be used as an object
  3  
  4  // An empty shell
  5  // [any]: The type of [this] is intentionally flexible here, because we assign
  6  // properties to the function itself, APRÈS, in its definition (see below) —
  7  // a schema that TypeScript cannot deduce on its own
  8  function f(this: any): void {
  9  
 10  }
 11  // to which properties are assigned from the outside
 12  (f as any).prop1 = "val1";
 13  (f as any).show = function (this: any) {
 14    console.log(this.prop1);
 15  };
 16  // use of f
 17  (f as any).show();
 18  
 19  // a function g that behaves like a class
 20  function g(this: any): void {
 21    this.prop2 = "val2";
 22    this.show = function (this: any) {
 23      console.log(this.prop2);
 24    };
 25  }
 26  // instantiation of the function with [new]
 27  new (g as any)().show();
  • lines 5–9: f is an “empty shell” function, typed as this: any</span>—this special annotation for the first parameter tells TypeScript the type of this inside the function, which is necessary here because properties are added to it from the outside, a pattern that TypeScript cannot deduce on its own;
  • Lines 12–15: Properties are assigned to f from outside—(f as any).prop1 = ...;
  • line 17: f.show() is called, not f()—this is indeed the notation for using an object, not a traditional function call;
  • lines 20–27: g defines this.prop2 and this.show within itself, just as a class constructor would;
  • line 29: <span style="color: #9a3412">new (g as any)() **instantiates **<span style="color: #9a3412">g as a class.
    • npx tsx fonctions/func-04.ts

    Execution result:

      1  val1
  2  val2
    Note: ES6 introduced the `class` keyword (see the chapter “Classes”), which allows you to achieve this result directly without using this functional workaround.

docs.title: 8.5. script [func-05]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates the use of [rest operator] (...), which collects all remaining arguments from a call into an array:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // rest operator
  3  function f(arg1: number, ...otherArgs: unknown[]): void {
  4    // first argument
  5    console.log("arg1=", arg1);
  6    // the other arguments
  7    let i = 0;
  8    otherArgs.forEach(element => {
  9      console.log("otherArguments[", i, "]=", element);
 10      i++;
 11    });
 12  }
 13  
 14  // call
 15  f(1, "deux", "trois", { x: 2, y: 3 })
  • Line 3: function f(arg1: number, ...otherArgs: unknown[]): void — otherArgs groups all arguments passed after arg1, regardless of their number. The <span style="color: #9a3412">unknown[] type is appropriate here because otherArgs intentionally mixes different types (strings and objects, in the call on line 15).

docs.title: 14. HTTP TypeScript clients of the tax calculation service
14.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Here we are creating a client, node.js, for version 14 of the tax calculation service (see the course “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples” for installation instructions and details about this server). We will examine two client structures:

  • Version 1, with a two-tier architecture [main, dao];
  • Version 2, with a three-tier architecture [main, métier, dao]—the business logic layer, which is server-side (PHP) in the original course, is moved to the client side (TypeScript) here.
Important: The scripts in this chapter assume, as in the previous chapter, that the course server PHP is running locally. In the environment where this document was prepared, this server is not available: the executions below show the actual result of this absence (connection error). The “expected” JSON responses, presented separately and clearly identified as such, are taken from the original 2019 document for illustrative purposes—they could not be re-verified here.

docs.title: 14.2. Client HTTP 1
docs.text:
This first client implements the layered structure [main, dao]:

  • the [dao] layer is implemented by a class, Dao1;
  • the [main] layer is a script that uses this class.

docs.title: 14.2.1. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // imports
  4  import { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
  5  import qs from 'qs'
  6  
  7  class Dao1 {
  8  
  9    private axios: AxiosInstance;
 10    private sessionCookieName: string;
 11    private sessionCookie: string;
 12  
 13    // constructor
 14    constructor(axios: AxiosInstance) {
 15      // axios library for making requests HTTP
 16      this.axios = axios;
 17      // session cookie
 18      this.sessionCookieName = "PHPSESSID";
 19      this.sessionCookie = '';
 20    }
 21  
 22    // session initialization
 23    async  initSession(): Promise<any> {
 24      // request options HHTP [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
 25      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 26        // [mise à jour TypeScript] URL included in [options.url] (see getRemoteData)
 27        url: 'main.php',
 28        method: "GET",
 29        // parameters of URL
 30        params: {
 31          action: 'init-session',
 32          type: 'json'
 33        }
 34      };
 35      // Execution of the query HTTP
 36      return await this.getRemoteData(options);
 37    }
 38  
 39    async  authentifierUtilisateur(user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
 40      // options for the HHTP request [post /main.php?action=authentifier-utilisateur]
 41      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 42        url: 'main.php',
 43        method: "POST",
 44        headers: {
 45          'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
 46        },
 47        // body of the POST
 48        data: qs.stringify({
 49          user: user,
 50          password: password
 51        }),
 52        // parameters of the URL
 53        params: {
 54          action: 'authentifier-utilisateur'
 55        }
 56      };
 57      // Execution of the query HTTP
 58      return await this.getRemoteData(options);
 59    }
 60  
 61    // tax calculation
 62    async  calculerImpot(marié: string, enfants: number, salaire: number): Promise<any> {
 63      // HHTP request options
 64      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 65        url: 'main.php',
 66        method: "POST",
 67        headers: {
 68          'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
 69        },
 70        // body of the POST
 71        data: qs.stringify({
 72          marié: marié,
 73          enfants: enfants,
 74          salaire: salaire
 75        }),
 76        // URL parameters
 77        params: {
 78          action: 'calculer-impot'
 79        }
 80      };
 81      // execution of the request HTTP
 82      const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
 83      // result
 84      return data;
 85    }
 86  
 87    // list of simulations
 88    async  listeSimulations(): Promise<any> {
 89      // options for the query HHTP
 90      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 91        url: 'main.php',
 92        method: "GET",
 93        // parameters for URL
 94        params: {
 95          action: 'lister-simulations'
 96        },
 97      };
 98      // HTTP query execution
 99      const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
100      // Result
101      return data;
102    }
103  
104    // list of simulations
105    async  supprimerSimulation(index: number): Promise<any> {
106      // options for the query HHTP
107      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
108        url: 'main.php',
109        method: "GET",
110        // parameters for URL
111        params: {
112          action: 'supprimer-simulation',
113          numéro: index
114        },
115      };
116      // HTTP query execution
117      const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
118      // Result
119      return data;
120    }
121  
122    async  getRemoteData(options: AxiosRequestConfig): Promise<any> {
123      // for the session cookie
124      if (!options.headers) {
125        options.headers = {} as any;
126      }
127      (options.headers as any).Cookie = this.sessionCookie;
128      // Execution of the HTTP request
129      let response: AxiosResponse;
130      try {
131        // asynchronous request
132        response = await this.axios.request(options);
133      } catch (error: any) {
134        // The parameter [error] is an exception instance—it can take various forms
135        if (error.response) {
136          // the server response is in [error.response]
137          response = error.response;
138        } else {
139          // The error is re-triggered
140          throw error;
141        }
142      }
143      // response is the entire HTTP response from the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
144      // retrieves the session cookie if it exists
145      const setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
146      if (setCookie) {
147        // setCookie is an array
148        // search for the session cookie in this array
149        let trouvé = false;
150        let i = 0;
151        while (!trouvé && i < setCookie.length) {
152          // Search for the session cookie
153          const results = RegExp('^(' + this.sessionCookieName + '.+?);').exec(setCookie[i]);
154          if (results) {
155            // The session cookie is stored
156            // eslint-disable-next-line require-atomic-updates
157            this.sessionCookie = results[1];
158            // Found it
159            trouvé = true;
160          } else {
161            // next element
162            i++;
163          }
164        }
165      }
166      // the server response is in [response.data]
167      return response.data;
168    }
169  }
170  
171  // exporting the class
172  export default Dao1;
  • Lines 8–10: The class has three private properties: axios (the instance passed by the calling code), sessionCookieName (the name of the session cookie—PHPSESSID, specific to PHP), sessionCookie (the cookie actually received, stored for subsequent requests);
  • lines 60–73: calculerImpot (married, children, salary) posts these three parameters to main.php?action=calculate-tax, and returns the server’s response JSON as an object TypeScript;
  • lines 122–160: getRemoteData centralizes the execution of requests: it adds the current session cookie to each outgoing request (line 126), then, upon receipt, searches for and stores any new session cookie in the response’s Set-Cookie header (lines 141–159)—manually handling what a browser would do automatically.

docs.title: 14.2.2. The [main1] script
docs.text:
This script chains together a series of calls to the server via the Dao1 class: session initialization, authentication, three tax calculations (in parallel), a list of simulations, and the deletion of one of them:

  1  
  2  // importing axios
  3  import axios from 'axios';
  4  // importing the Dao class
  5  import Dao from './Dao1.js';
  6  
  7  
  8  // asynchronous function [main]
  9  async function main(): Promise<void> {
 10    // Axios configuration
 11    axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
 12    axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost/php7/scripts-web/impots/version-14';
 13    // [dao] layer instantiation
 14    const dao = new Dao(axios);
 15    // using the layer [dao]
 16    try {
 17      // session initialization
 18      log("-----------init-session");
 19      let response = await dao.initSession();
 20      log(response);
 21      // authentication
 22      log("-----------authentifier-utilisateur");
 23      response = await dao.authentifierUtilisateur("admin", "admin");
 24      log(response);
 25      // tax calculations
 26      log("-----------calculer-impot x 3");
 27      response = await Promise.all([
 28        dao.calculerImpot("oui", 2, 45000),
 29        dao.calculerImpot("non", 2, 45000),
 30        dao.calculerImpot("non", 1, 30000)
 31      ]);
 32      log(response);
 33      // List of simulations
 34      log("-----------liste-des-simulations");
 35      response = await dao.listeSimulations();
 36      log(response);
 37      // delete a simulation
 38      log("-----------suppression simulation n° 1");
 39      response = await dao.supprimerSimulation(1);
 40      log(response);
 41    } catch (error: any) {
 42      // log the error
 43      console.log("erreur=", error.message);
 44    }
 45  }
 46  
 47  // log jSON
 48  function log(object: unknown): void {
 49    console.log(JSON.stringify(object, null, 2));
 50  }
 51  
 52  // execution
 53  main();
  • Lines 9–10: Default Axios configuration—2-second timeout, base URL from server version 14;
  • lines 26–30: the three tax calculations are requested in parallel with Promise.all([...])—execution waits until all three results are obtained;
  • lines 46–48: The log displays the string JSON for an object, indented by two spaces, for easier reading.
