docs.title: 14.3. Client HTTP 2
docs.text: In this second version, the [métier] layer—which calculates the tax—is moved from the PHP server to the TypeScript client. Unlike the PHP7 course, the main layer does not need to go through the business layer to reach the DAO layer: these are two independent centers of expertise—the main layer accesses the DAO layer for server data and the business layer for calculations, while the business layer never calls upon the DAO layer.

docs.title: 14.3.1. The [Métier] class
docs.text:
The tax calculation logic closely follows that of class PHP, which is covered in the course “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples "— we will not go into detail about it again here; we are only interested in its translation into TypeScript:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // Business Class
  4  class Métier {
  5  
  6    // [any]: the exact structure of the data sent by the tax server (rates, thresholds, etc.)
  7    // is not documented here; we are therefore intentionally keeping this type flexible
  8    taxAdminData: any;
  9  
 10    // manufacturer
 11    constructor(taxAdmindata: any) {
 12      // this.taxAdminData: data from the tax authority
 13      this.taxAdminData = taxAdmindata;
 14    }
 15  
 16    // tax calculation
 17    // --------------------------------------------------------------------------
 18    calculerImpot(marié: string, enfants: number, salaire: number): any {
 19      // Married: Yes, No
 20      // children: number of children
 21      // Salary: annual salary
 22      // this.taxAdminData: Data from the tax authorities
 23      //
 24      // tax calculation with children
 25      const result1 = this.calculerImpot2(marié, enfants, salaire);
 26      const impot1 = result1["impôt"];
 27      // tax calculation without children
 28      let result2, impot2, plafondDemiPart;
 29      if (enfants !== 0) {
 30        result2 = this.calculerImpot2(marié, 0, salaire);
 31        impot2 = result2["impôt"];
 32        // Application of the family quotient cap
 33        plafondDemiPart = this.taxAdminData.plafondQfDemiPart;
 34        if (enfants < 3) {
 35          // PLAFOND_QF_DEMI_PART euros for the first two children
 36          impot2 = impot2 - enfants * plafondDemiPart;
 37        } else {
 38          // PLAFOND_QF_DEMI_PART euros for the first two children, double that amount for subsequent children
 39          impot2 = impot2 - 2 * plafondDemiPart - (enfants - 2) * 2 * plafondDemiPart;
 40        }
 41      } else {
 42        // no tax recalculation
 43        impot2 = impot1;
 44        result2 = result1;
 45      }
 46      // the highest tax amount is used in [impot1, impot2]
 47      let impot, taux, surcôte;
 48      if (impot1 > impot2) {
 49        impot = impot1;
 50        taux = result1["taux"];
 51        surcôte = result1["surcôte"];
 52      } else {
 53        surcôte = impot2 - impot1 + result2["surcôte"];
 54        impot = impot2;
 55        taux = result2["taux"];
 56      }
 57      // Calculation of a possible tax deduction
 58      const décôte = this.getDecôte(marié, impot);
 59      impot -= décôte;
 60      // Calculation of a potential tax reduction
 61      const réduction = this.getRéduction(marié, salaire, enfants, impot);
 62      impot -= réduction;
 63      // Result
 64      return {
 65        "impôt": Math.floor(impot), "surcôte": surcôte, "décôte": décôte, "réduction": réduction,
 66        "taux": taux
 67      };
 68    }
 69  
 70    // --------------------------------------------------------------------------
 71    calculerImpot2(marié: string, enfants: number, salaire: number): any {
 72      // married: yes, no
 73      // children: number of children
 74      // Salary: annual salary
 75      // this->taxAdminData: data from the tax authorities
 76      // 
 77      // number of shares
 78      marié = marié.toLowerCase();
 79      let nbParts;
 80      if (marié === "oui") {
 81        nbParts = enfants / 2 + 2;
 82      } else {
 83        nbParts = enfants / 2 + 1;
 84      }
 85      // 1 share per child starting with the third
 86      if (enfants >= 3) {
 87        // half an additional share for each child starting with the third
 88        nbParts += 0.5 * (enfants - 2);
 89      }
 90      // taxable income
 91      const revenuImposable = this.getRevenuImposable(salaire);
 92      // surcharge
 93      let surcôte = Math.floor(revenuImposable - 0.9 * salaire);
 94      // for rounding issues
 95      if (surcôte < 0) {
 96        surcôte = 0;
 97      }
 98      // family quotient
 99      const quotient = revenuImposable / nbParts;
100      // tax calculation
101      const limites = this.taxAdminData.limites;
102      const coeffR = this.taxAdminData.coeffR;
103      const coeffN = this.taxAdminData.coeffN;
104      // is placed at the end of the limits table to terminate the following loop
105      limites[limites.length - 1] = quotient;
106      // looks up the tax rate
107      let i = 0;
108      while (quotient > limites[i]) {
109        i++;
110      }
111      // Since the family quotient was placed at the end of the limits table, the previous loop
112      // cannot go beyond the bounds of the array
113      // Now we can calculate the tax
114      const impôt = Math.floor(revenuImposable * coeffR[i] - nbParts * coeffN[i]);
115      // Result
116      return { "impôt": impôt, "surcôte": surcôte, "taux": coeffR[i] };
117    }
118  
119    // revenuImposable = annualSalary - deduction
120    // The deduction has a minimum and a maximum
121    getRevenuImposable(salaire: number): number {
122      // 10% salary deduction
123      let abattement = 0.1 * salaire;
124      // This deduction cannot exceed taxAdminData.getAbattementDixPourCentMax()
125      if (abattement > this.taxAdminData.abattementDixPourCentMax) {
126        abattement = this.taxAdminData.abattementDixPourcentMax;
127      }
128      // The deduction cannot be less than taxAdminData.getAbattementDixPourcentMin()
129      if (abattement < this.taxAdminData.abattementDixPourcentMin) {
130        abattement = this.taxAdminData.abattementDixPourcentMin;
131      }
132      // taxable income
133      const revenuImposable = salaire - abattement;
134      // net income
135      return Math.floor(revenuImposable);
136    }
137  
138    // calculates any discount
139    getDecôte(marié: string, impots: number): number {
140      // Initially, a zero discount
141      let décôte = 0;
142      // maximum tax amount to qualify for the discount
143      let plafondImpôtPourDécôte = marié === "oui" ?
144        this.taxAdminData.plafondImpotCouplePourDecote :
145        this.taxAdminData.plafondImpotCelibatairePourDecote;
146      let plafondDécôte;
147      if (impots < plafondImpôtPourDécôte) {
148        // maximum discount amount
149        plafondDécôte = marié === "oui" ?
150          this.taxAdminData.plafondDecoteCouple :
151          this.taxAdminData.plafondDecoteCelibataire;
152        // theoretical discount
153        décôte = plafondDécôte - 0.75 * impots;
154        // The discount cannot exceed the tax amount
155        if (décôte > impots) {
156          décôte = impots;
157        }
158        // No discount <0
159        if (décôte < 0) {
160          décôte = 0;
161        }
162      }
163      // Result
164      return Math.ceil(décôte);
165    }
166  
167    // calculates a possible reduction
168    getRéduction(marié: string, salaire: number, enfants: number, impots: number): number {
169      // the income threshold for eligibility for the 20% reduction
170      let plafondRevenuPourRéduction = marié === "oui" ?
171        this.taxAdminData.plafondRevenusCouplePourReduction :
172        this.taxAdminData.plafondRevenusCelibatairePourReduction;
173      plafondRevenuPourRéduction += enfants * this.taxAdminData.valeurReducDemiPart;
174      if (enfants > 2) {
175        plafondRevenuPourRéduction += (enfants - 2) * this.taxAdminData.valeurReducDemiPart;
176      }
177      // taxable income
178      const revenuImposable = this.getRevenuImposable(salaire);
179      // reduction
180      let réduction = 0;
181      if (revenuImposable < plafondRevenuPourRéduction) {
182        // 20% reduction
183        réduction = 0.2 * impots;
184      }
185      // result
186      return Math.ceil(réduction);
187    }
188  }
189  
190  // export the class
191  export default Métier;
  • Line 7: taxAdminData: any — the exact structure of the data sent by the tax server (rates, thresholds, etc.) is not documented; we are therefore intentionally keeping this type flexible rather than speculating on an uncertain interface;
  • Unlike version PHP, the constructor (line 10) no longer receives an instance of the DAO layer—the business layer, in this case, is completely independent of the network; the calling code provides it with the tax data directly;
  • The executeBatchImpots method from the original PHP code has not been included: it used to save results to the file system, an operation that cannot be replicated exactly in a browser.

docs.title: 14.3.2. The [Dao2] class
docs.text:
The DAO layer in this version adds a method, [getAdminData], which retrieves the tax data required by the business layer from the server:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // imports
  4  import { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
  5  import qs from 'qs'
  6  
  7  class Dao2 {
  8  
  9    private axios: AxiosInstance;
 10    private sessionCookieName: string;
 11    private sessionCookie: string;
 12  
 13    // constructor
 14    constructor(axios: AxiosInstance) {
 15      this.axios = axios;
 16      // session cookie
 17      this.sessionCookieName = "PHPSESSID";
 18      this.sessionCookie = '';
 19    }
 20  
 21    // session initialization
 22    async  initSession(): Promise<any> {
 23      // request options HHTP [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
 24      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 25        url: 'main.php',
 26        method: "GET",
 27        // URL parameters
 28        params: {
 29          action: 'init-session',
 30          type: 'json'
 31        }
 32      };
 33      // Execution of the query HTTP
 34      return await this.getRemoteData(options);
 35    }
 36  
 37    async  authentifierUtilisateur(user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
 38      // request options HHTP [post /main.php?action=authentifier-utilisateur]
 39      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 40        url: 'main.php',
 41        method: "POST",
 42        headers: {
 43          'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
 44        },
 45        // body of the POST
 46        data: qs.stringify({
 47          user: user,
 48          password: password
 49        }),
 50        // URL parameters
 51        params: {
 52          action: 'authentifier-utilisateur'
 53        }
 54      };
 55      // execution of the query HTTP
 56      return await this.getRemoteData(options);
 57    }
 58  
 59    async getAdminData(): Promise<any> {
 60      // options for the query HHTP  [get /main.php?action=get-admindata]
 61      const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
 62        url: 'main.php',
 63        method: "GET",
 64        // parameters for URL
 65        params: {
 66          action: 'get-admindata'
 67        }
 68      };
 69      // Execution of the query HTTP
 70      const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
 71      // result
 72      return data;
 73    }
 74  
 75    async  getRemoteData(options: AxiosRequestConfig): Promise<any> {
 76      // for the session cookie
 77      if (!options.headers) {
 78        options.headers = {} as any;
 79      }
 80      (options.headers as any).Cookie = this.sessionCookie;
 81      // Execution of the HTTP request
 82      let response: AxiosResponse;
 83      try {
 84        // asynchronous request
 85        response = await this.axios.request(options);
 86      } catch (error: any) {
 87        // The parameter [error] is an exception instance—it can take various forms
 88        if (error.response) {
 89          // the server's response is in [error.response]
 90          response = error.response;
 91        } else {
 92          // The error is re-triggered
 93          throw error;
 94        }
 95      }
 96      // response is the entire response HTTP from the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
 97      // retrieves the session cookie if it exists
 98      const setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
 99      if (setCookie) {
100        // setCookie is an array
101        // search for the session cookie in this array
102        let trouvé = false;
103        let i = 0;
104        while (!trouvé && i < setCookie.length) {
105          // Search for the session cookie
106          const results = RegExp('^(' + this.sessionCookieName + '.+?);').exec(setCookie[i]);
107          if (results) {
108            // The session cookie is stored
109            // eslint-disable-next-line require-atomic-updates
110            this.sessionCookie = results[1];
111            // Found it
112            trouvé = true;
113          } else {
114            // next element
115            i++;
116          }
117        }
118      }
119      // the server response is in [response.data]
120      return response.data;
121    }
122  }
123  
124  // export of the class
125  export default Dao2;

docs.title: 14.4. Client HTTP 3
docs.text: In this final section, we load the HTTP 2 client into a browser. While node.js natively executes TypeScript via tsx, this is not the case for browsers: a tool is needed to compile TypeScript into JavaScript, then assemble the whole thing into a single file that can be used by a HTML page. This is the role of [webpack].

docs.title: 14.4.1. Changes to the toolset since 2019
docs.text:
The original document (2019) used [babel-loader] to transpile the ES6 code into ES5, which is compatible with older browsers. Since our project is now written in TypeScript, we are replacing babel-loader with [ts-loader], which natively supports the TypeScript syntax (types, interfaces, etc.)—something that Babel completely ignores.

The project’s [webpack.config.js] file (client folder impots/client http 3):

/* eslint-disable */

const path = require("path");
const webpack = require("webpack");

/*
 * SplitChunksPlugin is enabled by default and replaced
 * deprecated CommonsChunkPlugin. It automatically identifies modules which
 * should be splitted of chunk by heuristics using module duplication count and
 * module category (i. e. node_modules). And splits the chunks…
 *
 * It is safe to remove "splitChunks" from the generated configuration
 * and was added as an educational example.
 *
 * https://webpack.js.org/plugins/split-chunks-plugin/
 *
 */

const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require("html-webpack-plugin");

/*
 * We've enabled HtmlWebpackPlugin for you! This generates a html
 * page for you when you compile webpack, which will make you start
 * developing and prototyping faster.
 *
 * https://github.com/jantimon/html-webpack-plugin
 *
 */

// [mise à jour TypeScript] The source files are now in .ts format: Webpack must
// resolve (resolve.extensions) and compile them with [ts-loader] instead of
// [babel-loader] (which does not support the TypeScript syntax: types, interfaces, etc.)
module.exports = {
  mode: "development",
   //entry: "./src/mainjs",
  entry: "./src/main3.ts",
  output: {
    filename: "[name].[chunkhash].js",
    path: path.resolve(__dirname, "dist")
  },

  resolve: {
    extensions: [".ts", ".js"]
  },

  plugins: [new webpack.ProgressPlugin(), new HtmlWebpackPlugin()],

  module: {
    rules: [
      {
        test: /\.ts$/,
        include: [path.resolve(__dirname, "src")],
        loader: "ts-loader"
      }
    ]
  },

  optimization: {
    splitChunks: {
      cacheGroups: {
        vendors: {
          priority: -10,
          test: /[\\/]node_modules[\\/]/
        }
      },

      chunks: "async",
      minChunks: 1,
      minSize: 30000,
      name: true
    }
  },

  devServer: {
    open: true
  }
};
  • line 37: entry: "./src/main3.ts" — webpack starts with this file and follows all its imports to build the final bundle;
  • lines 41–43: resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] } — tells Webpack to also resolve .ts files even if the extension isn’t specified in the imports;
  • lines 47–53: the rule that associates every .ts file in the src folder with the [ts-loader] loader — this is the direct replacement for babel-loader mentioned above.

docs.title: 14.4.3. Compilation and Execution
docs.text:
The package.json file defines two npm tasks:

  • [npm run build] — compiles the project; the resulting files are placed in dist/ (a main.<hash>.js file, and a index.html file that automatically integrates it using the html-webpack-plugin);
  • [npm start] — starts webpack-dev-server: compiles the project and serves it at http://localhost:8080, with the page automatically reloading every time a source file is saved.
Reminder: As with the previous chapters, this client assumes that the PHP tax calculation server is running locally—without it, the page loaded in the browser will display a network error in its console, just like the node.js scripts from the previous chapters.

docs.title: 14.5. Conclusion
docs.text: This chapter has shown how the same business logic foundation (DAO and business layers) can be executed both from the command line (node.js, chapters “Client HTTP 1” and “Client HTTP 2”) as in a browser (chapter “Client HTTP 3”), using a suitable compilation tool—in this case, webpack and ts-loader. This TypeScript foundation is the starting point for modern front-end frameworks (React, Vue, Angular...), which are built on the same building blocks: modules, classes, async/await, and a build tool that assembles them for the browser.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a rewrite by Anthropic’s IA Claude, in 2026, of the course “Introduction to the ECMASCRIPT 6 Language Through Examples” written by Serge Tahé in October 2019 [https://stahe.github.io/ecmascript6-oct-2019/]. This took place in two stages:

  • I gave IA Claude the VSCode project based on the original 2019 document and asked him to rewrite all the scripts in TypeScript;
  • then I gave him the ODT file from the original course and asked him to adapt it to the new scripts;

This document is the result of those two steps. From this point on, IA Claude will be speaking.

Serge Tahé, September 2026

==

The language has evolved significantly since 2019: ECMAScript has gone through editions from 2020 to 2026, and a companion language, [TypeScript], has established itself as the safest way to write JavaScript on a large scale. This rewrite closely follows the structure and instructional approach of the original document—a script, its code, a line-by-line explanation, and its execution—but:

  • all scripts are now written in [TypeScript] rather than in pure JavaScript;
  • the explanations cover not only the language’s syntax but also its types and the differences from JavaScript;
  • new chapters have been added to cover the new features introduced between 2020 and 2026: optional chaining, classes with private fields, top-level await, Object.groupBy, Array.fromAsync, and the very latest additions from ECMAScript 2026 (Math.sumPrecise, Iterator.concat, Error.isError...);
  • a chapter is devoted to [Temporal], the modern successor to the Date object;
  • the VSCode runtime screenshots from the original document have been replaced with the actual, verified output of each script, using tsx on Node.js 26.

Like the original document, this one refers to a tax calculation server written in PHP 7 (see the course “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples”). The final chapters build, in TypeScript, a client for this server—first a console application, structured in layers using [UI, métier, dao], and then a client running in a browser using [webpack].

This document requires active reading: to understand a script, you must read its code, its comments, and the actual result of its execution.

docs.title: 1.1. Target Audience and Prerequisites
docs.text: This document is intended for beginners in TypeScript who are already familiar with the basics of programming (variables, loops, functions, conditional structures) in another language. No prior knowledge of JavaScript or TypeScript is required.

docs.title: 1.2. Organization of the Example Project
docs.text:
All scripts presented in this document belong to a single VSCode project, organized into one folder per chapter (basics, arrays, objects, strings, regexp, functions, exceptions, modules, async, http, classes, new features, ecmascript-2026, temporal, tax client). Each script is a .ts file that can be run directly with the following command from the project root:

npx tsx chemin/vers/le/script.ts
Tip: The README.md files in each project folder provide a condensed summary of the instructional content in this document—they can serve as a quick reference once you’ve read the document.

docs.title: 5. Literal Objects
docs.text: Here, we refer to “literal objects” as objects defined directly in the code, as opposed to instances of [class] (discussed in the chapter “Classes”). The scripts for this chapter are located in the [objets] folder of the project.

docs.title: 5.1. script [obj-01]
docs.text:
As with arrays, an object is manipulated via a pointer. In TypeScript, you must also describe the object’s structure using an interface before you can dynamically add properties to it.

  1  'use strict';
  2  // an empty object
  3  // interface: you declare in advance the properties you’re going to add dynamically,
  4  // because TypeScript (unlike JavaScript) requires knowing the structure of an object
  5  interface Obj1 {
  6    prop1?: string;
  7    prop2?: number[];
  8    prop3?: boolean;
  9    [clé: string]: unknown;
 10  }
 11  const obj1: Obj1 = {};
 12  // the object’s properties can be created dynamically
 13  obj1.prop1 = "abcd";
 14  console.log('obj1=', obj1);
 15  // another property
 16  obj1.prop2 = [1, 2, 3];
 17  console.log("obj1=", obj1);
 18  // another property with a different notation
 19  obj1['prop3'] = true;
 20  console.log("obj1=", obj1);
 21  // obj1 is a reference to the object (pointer), not the object itself
 22  const obj2: Obj1 = obj1;
 23  // obj2 and obj1 point to the same object
 24  obj2.prop1 = "xyzt";
 25  console.log("obj1=", obj1);
 26  console.log("obj2=", obj2);
 27  // Properties can be variables
 28  const var1: string = 'prop1';
 29  console.log('prop1=', obj1[var1]);

docs.title: 5.3. script [obj-03]
docs.text:
This script introduces the concept of getters and setters for an object's property:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // getters and setters of an object
  3  interface PersonneAvecNom {
  4    _nom?: string;
  5    nom: string;
  6  }
  7  const personne: PersonneAvecNom = {
  8    // getter
  9    get nom() {
 10      console.log("getter nom");
 11      return this._nom as string;
 12    },
 13    // setter
 14    set nom(unNom: string) {
 15      console.log("setter nom");
 16      this._nom = unNom;
 17    }
 18  };
 19  // setter
 20  personne.nom = "Hercule";
 21  // getter
 22  console.log(personne.nom);
 23  // the object itself
 24  console.log("personne=", personne);
 25  // this does not prevent direct access to the property [_nom]
 26  personne._nom = "xyz";
 27  console.log("personne=", personne);
  • Lines 3–6: [interface] and PersonneAvecNom declare _nom as an optional property (prefixed with an underscore by convention, to indicate that it is a “private” property, even though TypeScript does not prevent access to it—see true encapsulation with #field in the chapter “Classes”);
  • lines 8–11: [getter]—using the <span style="color: #9a3412">get keyword rather than a function—returns the value of _nom;
  • lines 13–16: [setter]—the set</span> keyword—receives the assigned value and can validate it before storing it;
  • line 19: personne.nom = "Hercule" implicitly calls the setter;
  • line 21: personne.nom implicitly calls the getter;
  • line 24: nothing prevents direct access to _nom—encapsulation by convention depends on the developer’s discipline.

  2  getter nom
  3  Hercule
  4  personne= { nom: [Getter/Setter], _nom: 'Hercule' }
  5  personne= { nom: [Getter/Setter], _nom: 'xyz' }

    Note that [console.log] displays [Getter/Setter] to indicate that "nom" is managed by accessors rather than being a direct value.

docs.text:
This script demonstrates how to iterate through an object's properties without knowing their names in advance:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // An object can have properties of type [function]
  4  interface PersonneAvecToString {
  5    prénom: string;
  6    âge: number;
  7    père: { prénom: string; âge: number };
  8    mère: { prénom: string; âge: number };
  9    toString: () => string;
 10    // signature index required to enable the dynamic traversal for..in below
 11    [clé: string]: unknown;
 12  }
 13  let personne: PersonneAvecToString = {
 14    // properties
 15    prénom: "martin",
 16    âge: 12,
 17    père: {
 18      prénom: "paul",
 19      âge: 45
 20    },
 21    mère: {
 22      prénom: "micheline",
 23      âge: 42
 24    },
 25    // method
 26    toString: function () {
 27      return JSON.stringify(this);
 28    }
 29  }
 30  
 31  // usage
 32  console.log(personne);
 33  // properties
 34  console.log("-----------------------");
 35  for (const key in personne) {
 36    // eslint-disable-next-line no-prototype-builtins
 37    if (personne.hasOwnProperty(key)) {
 38      const element = personne[key];
 39      console.log(key, "=", element);
 40    }
 41  }
 42  // to avoid the ESLint warning (1)
 43  console.log("-----------------------");
 44  for (const key in personne) {
 45    if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(personne, key)) {
 46      const element = personne[key];
 47      console.log(key, "=", element);
 48    }
 49  }
 50  // to avoid the ESLint warning (2)
 51  console.log("-----------------------");
 52  for (const key in personne) {
 53    // eslint-disable-next-line no-prototype-builtins
 54    if (personne.hasOwnProperty(key)) {
 55      const element = personne[key];
 56      console.log(key, "=", element);
 57    }
 58  }
  • Line 9: The index signature [clé: string]: unknown is required here so that TypeScript can grant dynamic access to person[key] from the loop for...in;
  • Lines 34–40: for (const key in person) iterates through the property names. The <span style="color: #9a3412">hasOwnProperty test eliminates any inherited properties (not present in this script, but a good practice to follow systematically);
  • this script offers three equivalent ways to write this test—the second (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(...)) is the most robust, while the third simply suppresses the corresponding ESLint warning. Since 2022, the Object.hasOwn() method (next chapter, obj-09) has made this choice unnecessary.

docs.title: 5.7. script [obj-07]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates object destructuring—a syntax that directly extracts properties into variables:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // deserialization
  3  
  4  interface NomPrénom {
  5    nom: string;
  6    prénom: string;
  7  }
  8  
  9  // literals
 10  const obj1: NomPrénom = {
 11    nom: "martin",
 12    prénom: "jean"
 13  };
 14  
 15  // destructuring obj1 into variables [n,p]
 16  const { nom: n, prénom: p } = obj1;
 17  console.log("n=", n, "p=", p);
 18  
 19  // unpacking obj1 into variables [n2,p2]
 20  function f({ nom: n2, prénom: p2 }: NomPrénom): void {
 21    console.log("f-n2=", n2, "f-p2=", p2);
 22  }
 23  f(obj1);
 24  
 25  // unpacking obj1 into variables [nom,prénom]
 26  function g({ nom: nom, prénom: prénom }: NomPrénom): void {
 27    console.log("g-nom=", nom, "g-prénom=", prénom);
 28  }
 29  g(obj1);
 30  
 31  // unpacking obj1 into variables [nom,prénom]
 32  // using shorthand notation equivalent to h({last_name:last_name,first_name:first_name})
 33  function h({ nom, prénom }: NomPrénom): void {
 34    console.log("h-nom=", nom, "h-prénom=", prénom);
 35  }
 36  h(obj1);
  • Line 15: const { last_name: n, first_name: p } = obj1 creates two variables, n and p, equivalent to const n = obj1.nom; const p = obj1.prénom;
  • lines 18–21, 24–27, 30–33: destructuring also works directly on function parameters—very common in TypeScript/React for extracting properties from a configuration object or props;
  • line 33: function h({ firstName, lastName }: NomPrénom) is a shorthand for { firstName: firstName, lastName: lastName }—when the name of the created variable is identical to the property name, it can be omitted.

docs.title: 5.9. script [obj-09]
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] This script demonstrates three useful additions introduced since 2020: [Object.hasOwn], [structuredClone], and the combination of optional chaining with null coalescing on nested objects.

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] Object manipulation: some practical additions
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7  // 1) Object.hasOwn(object, property)  (ECMAScript 2022)
  8  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  9  // Previously, to determine whether a property belongs directly to an object (and is not
 10  // inherited through the prototype chain), we would write:
 11  //   objet.hasOwnProperty(property)               -> may crash if the object redefines hasOwnProperty
 12  //   Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(object, property)  -> correct but verbose (see objects/obj-06.js)
 13  // [Object.hasOwn] does this job simply and safely
 14  interface NomPrénom {
 15    nom: string;
 16    prénom: string;
 17    [clé: string]: unknown;
 18  }
 19  const personne: NomPrénom = { nom: "Dupont", prénom: "Jean" };
 20  
 21  console.log("Object.hasOwn(personne, 'nom') =", Object.hasOwn(personne, "nom"));
 22  console.log("Object.hasOwn(personne, 'âge') =", Object.hasOwn(personne, "âge"));
 23  
 24  // typical use in a property traversal
 25  console.log("-----------------------");
 26  for (const clé in personne) {
 27    if (Object.hasOwn(personne, clé)) {
 28      console.log(clé, "=", personne[clé]);
 29    }
 30  }
 31  
 32  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 33  // 2) structuredClone (object)  (Global API available since Node 17)
 34  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 35  // obj-08.js demonstrates shallow cloning using the spread operator [...obj]
 36  // but a spread only clones the first level: the subobjects remain shared!
 37  interface PersonneAvecAdresse {
 38    nom: string;
 39    adresse: { ville: string; codePostal: string };
 40  }
 41  const original: PersonneAvecAdresse = {
 42    nom: "Dupont",
 43    adresse: { ville: "Nantes", codePostal: "44000" }
 44  };
 45  
 46  // shallow cloning with spread
 47  const copieSuperficielle: PersonneAvecAdresse = { ...original };
 48  copieSuperficielle.adresse.ville = "Angers"; // also modifies the address of [original]!
 49  console.log("copie superficielle a modifié l'original :", original.adresse.ville === "Angers");
 50  
 51  // reset for the next test
 52  original.adresse.ville = "Nantes";
 53  
 54  // [structuredClone] performs a deep clone: all subobjects are copied
 55  const copieProfonde: PersonneAvecAdresse = structuredClone(original);
 56  copieProfonde.adresse.ville = "Angers";
 57  console.log("copie profonde n'a pas modifié l'original :", original.adresse.ville === "Nantes");
 58  console.log("original =", original);
 59  console.log("copieProfonde =", copieProfonde);
 60  
 61  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 62  // 3) Optional chaining + nullish checks on nested object methods
 63  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 64  // A very common combination in practice for reading a partial configuration
 65  interface ConfigurationApparence {
 66    apparence?: { thème?: string };
 67  }
 68  function afficheThème(configuration?: ConfigurationApparence): void {
 69    // if configuration, configuration.apparence or configuration.apparence.thème is missing,
 70    // it reverts to "clear" without ever crashing
 71    const thème = configuration?.apparence?.thème ?? "clair";
 72    console.log("thème =", thème);
 73  }
 74  afficheThème({ apparence: { thème: "sombre" } });
 75  afficheThème({ apparence: {} });
 76  afficheThème({});
 77  afficheThème(undefined);
  • [Object.hasOwn(objet, propriété)] (ES2022) is a better replacement for objet.hasOwnProperty(...) (see script obj-06): it’s easier to read, and you’ll never run into issues if the object redefines hasOwnProperty itself;
  • [structuredClone(objet)] (available natively since Node 17) performs a deep clone: unlike the spread { ...obj } in the obj-08 script, which copies only the first level, structuredClone also copies the subobjects—modifying the copy never modifies the original, at any level;
  • the function afficheThème combines ?. and ?? to read a multi-level, potentially incomplete configuration without ever crashing and with a clear fallback value.

docs.title: 5.10. Conclusion
docs.text: The scripts in this chapter have shown that the literal object TypeScript is similar to a class instance: you can define properties, methods, and getters/setters—with the added benefit of a [interface] that precisely describes its form at compile time. It is a dynamic object, comparable to a dictionary, whose elements can be of any type, including functions.

docs.title: 10. Modules
docs.text: The ECMAScript modules allow you to build applications structured into independent, reusable files, each of which exports the data it wishes to make available to others. The scripts in this chapter are located in the [modules] folder of the project.

docs.title: 10.1. [import-01, export-01] scripts
docs.text:
The [import-01] script uses the [export-01] module:

  1  ﻿// default export of an unnamed object
  2  export default {
  3    data: 2,
  4    do() {
  5      console.log(this.data);
  6    }
  7  };
  • [export default] exports an unnamed object—only one default export is allowed per module.
  1  'use strict';
  2  // Importing an object exported by default
  3  import export01 from './export-01.js';
  4  // Use of this object
  5  export01.do();
  6  // A default export can be imported under any name
  7  import data from './export-01.js';
  8  console.log(data.data);
  • Lines 3 and 7 import the module’s default export under two different names (export01, then data)—the name given to the import is arbitrary; it does not need to correspond to anything in the source module;
  • Once imported, the object can be used as if it had been defined locally.
npx tsx modules/import-01.ts

Execution result:

  1  2
  2  2

docs.text:
These scripts show that exporting a named object (previously stored in a variable) works exactly the same way:

  1  ﻿// default export of a named object
  2  const data = {
  3    data: 2,
  4    do() {
  5      console.log(this.data);
  6    }
  7  };
  8  // export
  9  export default data;

  1  'use strict';
  2  // Importing a default export object
  3  import module1 from './export-02.js';
  4  // Using this object
  5  module1.do();
  6  // You can import a default export under any name
  7  import module2 from './export-02.js';
  8  console.log(module2.data);

docs.title: 10.3. [import-03, export-03] scripts
docs.text:
A module can export multiple elements using the syntax <span style="color: #9a3412">export { element }:

  1  ﻿// multi-exports
  2  // export object
  3  const data = {
  4    data: 2,
  5    do() {
  6      console.log(this.data);
  7    }
  8  };
  9  // export function
 10  export { data };
 11  function doSomething(): void {
 12    console.log("doSomething");
 13  }
 14  export { doSomething };

  1  'use strict';
  2  // Importing a module [export03]
  3  import {data, doSomething} from './export-03.js';
  4  // using imports
  5  data.do();
  6  doSomething();
  7  // other syntax
  8  import * as module from './export-03.js';
  9  // using the import
 10  console.log(module.data);
 11  module.doSomething();
  • Line 3: Named imports use the exact names of the exported elements, enclosed in curly braces;
  • line 8: <span style="color: #9a3412">import \* as module from '...' imports all exported elements, grouped into a named object (here, <span style="color: #9a3412">module</span>).

docs.title: 10.4. [import-04, config-distante] scripts — top-level await
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] ECMAScript Version 2022 introduced top-level await: the ability to use <span style="color: #9a3412">await directly at the top level of a module, without wrapping it in an <span style="color: #9a3412">async function. Previously, you had to create an async “main” function and call it immediately (see the next chapter, script async-06).

The [config-distante] module simulates the loading of a remote configuration and uses top-level await:

  1  // Module simulating the reading of a remote configuration (e.g., network call)
  2  // Used by modules/import-04.js to illustrate top-level await
  3  
  4  interface Configuration {
  5    nomApplication: string;
  6    version: string;
  7  }
  8  
  9  // a function that simulates an asynchronous call (e.g., fetching a configuration file)
 10  function chargerDepuisLeRéseau(): Promise<Configuration> {
 11    return new Promise(resolve => {
 12      setTimeout(() => {
 13        resolve({ nomApplication: "cours ECMAScript", version: "2026" });
 14      }, 300);
 15    });
 16  }
 17  
 18  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2022] top-level await: you can use [await] directly
 19  // at the top level of a module, without wrapping it in an `async` function.
 20  // The module ENTIER (and any module that imports it) waits for this line to finish
 21  // before continuing: this is very useful for initializing a configuration
 22  // just once, when the module loads.
 23  console.log("[config-distante] chargement de la configuration en cours...");
 24  const configuration: Configuration = await chargerDepuisLeRéseau();
 25  console.log("[config-distante] configuration chargée");
 26  
 27  // The result is exported, already resolved (rather than a promise that needs to be re-resolved)
 28  export default configuration;

The script [import-04] imports this module:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] top-level await  (ECMAScript 2022)
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // Before ECMAScript 2022, it was impossible to use [await] outside
  7  // a [async] function: at the top level of a script, you had to create
  8  // an async "main" function and call it immediately (see async/async-06.js)
  9  
 10  // Note on execution order: with ES modules, the [import] are always
 11  // evaluated as AVANT—the code from the importing module—even if written on the first line.
 12  // This is why the logs for [config-distante.js] are displayed before this one,
 13  // even though the following line is literally placed before the import in this file.
 14  console.log("[import-04] avant l'import du module config-distante");
 15  
 16  // Thanks to the top-level `await` used in DANS config-distante.js, the import below
 17  // completes only after the configuration has finished loading: there is no need
 18  // to call .then() or create an async function here
 19  import configuration from './config-distante.js';
 20  
 21  console.log("[import-04] après l'import : la configuration est déjà disponible");
 22  console.log("configuration =", configuration);
 23  
 24  // you can also use [await] directly here, in this module, at the top level
 25  console.log("[import-04] attente de 200ms en top-level await...");
 26  await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
 27  console.log("[import-04] terminé");
  • Line 20: Thanks to the top-level await used **in **<span style="color: #9a3412">config-distante.ts</span>, the import on line 20 only completes once the configuration has finished loading—no need for .then() or an <span style="color: #9a3412">async function here;
  • ES modules are always evaluated before the code of the module that imports them, even if the import statement isn’t on the first line of the file: this is why the messages from config-distante.ts are displayed before those from import-04.ts, even though the latter is literally placed before the import in the file;
  • Line 26: You can also use <span style="color: #9a3412">await directly within <span style="color: #9a3412">import-04.ts itself, at its own top level.

docs.title: 15. New Features ECMAScript 2020–2024
docs.text:
The previous chapters have already covered, as we went along, most of the language features introduced since 2019—optional chaining and null coalescing (bases-09), Object.hasOwn and structuredClone (obj-09), new array methods (tab-05), replaceAll/matchAll (str-07), native private fields (class-05), Error with cause (excep-04), top-level await (import-04), and Promise extensions (async-07).

This chapter brings together the last two new features from ECMAScript 2024 that did not fit into any existing chapter: [Object.groupBy]/[Map.groupBy], and [Array.fromAsync]. The script is located in the [nouveautes] folder of the project.

docs.title: 15.1. script [groupBy-et-fromAsync]
docs.text:
1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] Object.groupBy, Map.groupBy, Array.fromAsync (ECMAScript 2024)
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7  // 1) Object.groupBy (array, fonctionDeGroupage)
  8  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  9  // Previously, to group the elements of an array based on a criterion, you had to
 10  // write your own loop using `reduce()` (see arrays/tab-04.js for `reduce`)
 11  interface Étudiant {
 12    nom: string;
 13    note: number;
 14  }
 15  const étudiants: Étudiant[] = [
 16    { nom: "Ana", note: 15 },
 17    { nom: "Léo", note: 8 },
 18    { nom: "Nora", note: 12 },
 19    { nom: "Théo", note: 6 },
 20    { nom: "Zoé", note: 17 }
 21  ];
 22  
 23  // the old way, using `reduce()`
 24  const groupesAvecReduce = étudiants.reduce((accumulateur: Record<string, Étudiant[]>, étudiant) => {
 25    const catégorie = étudiant.note >= 10 ? "admis" : "recalé";
 26    // if an array for this category doesn’t exist yet, create it
 27    (accumulateur[catégorie] ??= []).push(étudiant);
 28    return accumulateur;
 29  }, {});
 30  console.log("avec reduce :", groupesAvecReduce);
 31  
 32  // New way, much more readable, using Object.groupBy
 33  const groupes = Object.groupBy(étudiants, étudiant => (étudiant.note >= 10 ? "admis" : "recalé"));
 34  console.log("avec Object.groupBy :", groupes);
 35  console.log("admis =", groupes.admis);
 36  console.log("recalés =", groupes.recalé);
 37  
 38  // Map.groupBy works the same way, but returns a [Map] rather than a literal object
 39  // is useful when the grouping keys are not strings (e.g., objects, numbers)
 40  const groupesEnMap = Map.groupBy(étudiants, étudiant => étudiant.note >= 10);
 41  console.log("avec Map.groupBy, clé [true] (admis) =", groupesEnMap.get(true));
 42  console.log("avec Map.groupBy, clé [false] (recalés) =", groupesEnMap.get(false));
 43  
 44  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 45  // 2) Array.fromAsync(itérableAsynchrone)
 46  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 47  // Array.from() (ES2015) knows how to construct an array from a synchronous iterable
 48  // Array.fromAsync() can do the same thing from an iterable ASYNCHRONE,
 49  // that is, a source that produces its elements one by one over time
 50  // (for example: reading a network stream page by page)
 51  
 52  // an asynchronous generator that produces 3 values, with a short delay between each one
 53  async function* générateurDePages(): AsyncGenerator<string> {
 54    for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
 55      // we simulate a network wait before each page
 56      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
 57      yield `page ${i}`;
 58    }
 59  }
 60  
 61  async function démoFromAsync(): Promise<void> {
 62    console.log("--- Array.fromAsync ---");
 63    // Without Array.fromAsync, we would have had to write a manual "for await...of" loop
 64    const pages = await Array.fromAsync(générateurDePages());
 65    console.log("pages =", pages);
 66  }
 67  
 68  démoFromAsync();
  • [Object.groupBy(tableau, fonction)] groups the elements of an array based on the result of a sorting function—much more readable than the manual implementation using <span style="color: #9a3412">reduce()</span> (compare the two implementations, lines 12–18 and line 33);
  • the result of Object.groupBy is an object without a prototype ([Object: null prototype])—a detail visible at runtime, which avoids certain pitfalls related to properties inherited from Object.prototype (such as toString, hasOwnProperty...) if a category were to bear that name;
  • [Map.groupBy] works identically but returns a Map rather than a literal object—essential whenever the grouping keys are not strings (in this case, booleans);
  • [Array.fromAsync(itérableAsynchrone)] constructs an array from an asynchronous source—an async function\* generator, for example—without having to write a manual for loop yourself to accumulate the results.

docs.title: 15.2. Summary Table
docs.text:
Let’s summarize, by version of ECMAScript, all the new features presented in this course since the “Basics” chapter:

  • [ES2020]: optional chaining ?., null coalescing ??, BigInt, Promise.allSettled, String.matchAll;
  • [ES2021]: logical assignment ||=/&&=/??=, numeric separators 1_000_000, Promise.any, String.replaceAll;
  • [ES2022]: private fields and methods #name, static initialization blocks, Object.hasOwn, Array.at, top-level await, Error with cause;
  • [ES2023]: findLast/findLastIndex, immutable methods toSorted/toReversed/toSpliced/with;
  • [ES2024]: Object.groupBy/Map.groupBy, Array.fromAsync, Promise.withResolvers, String.isWellFormed/toWellFormed.

The following chapters describe the new features of ECMAScript 2026, as well as [Temporal], the modern replacement for the Date object.

docs.title: 16. New Features in ECMAScript 2026
docs.text: ECMAScript 2026 (17th edition of the language) was officially finalized by TC39 in 2026. According to the official specification text (https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/), this edition added: Math.sumPrecise to add a set of numbers while minimizing loss of precision; Iterator.concat to chain iterators; Array.fromAsync (already introduced in the previous chapter); Error.isError to reliably identify error objects; methods on Map.prototype and WeakMap.prototype to provide a default value during a read operation; methods on Uint8Array for hexadecimal and Base64 conversions; a context parameter for the callbacks of JSON.parse; and JSON.rawJSON for fine-tuning the output of JSON.stringify.

docs.title: 16.1. ⚠️ An important warning before you begin
docs.text:
Stage 4 of TC39 guarantees that a feature’s behavior will no longer change, but does not guarantee its immediate availability in all JavaScript engines. While preparing this chapter, one concrete example clearly demonstrated this: [Math.sumPrecise] causes the error “TypeError: Math.sumPrecise is not a function,” even on recent versions of Node.js. This is not a bug in this course: V8 (the engine used by Node and Chrome) simply has not yet implemented this feature—unlike Firefox, Safari, and Bun, which already have it (source: official issue ticket for the TypeScript repository, github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/63427).

That’s why each script in this chapter uses typeof</span> to check for itself whether the feature it demonstrates is available before using it, and displays a clear message if it isn’t—rather than crashing abruptly. This is a best practice in itself when using very recent language features. Important: All the scripts in this chapter have actually been run in the course preparation environment (Node.js 22); some of them display the message “not available” there, which is an actual result and not an assumption. On your machine, with a different version of Node.js, some of these scripts may display an actual result rather than this message—feel free to compare.

docs.title: 16.2. [01-math-sumPrecise] script
docs.text:
1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Math.sumPrecise()
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [mise à jour] at the time this script was written, V8 (i.e., Node.js and Chrome)
  6  // does not implement PAS ENCORE Math.sumPrecise, whereas Firefox, Safari, and Bun
  7  // already have it. This is a concrete example of the gap that can exist between
  8  // "the feature has been included in the official language specification"
  9  // and “all browsers have actually implemented it”: Stage 4
 10  // of TC39 (achieved on 07/28/2025 for this feature) guarantees that the
 11  // behavior will not change anymore, but does not guarantee PAS immediate availability
 12  // everywhere. See ecmascript-2026/README.md for details and
 13  // source code.
 14  // To check for yourself whether TON Node.js already has this feature:
 15  //   node -e "console.log(typeof Math.sumPrecise)"
 16  
 17  // adding floating-point numbers with + accumulates rounding errors,
 18  // because each number is represented in binary in an imprecise way
 19  const nombres: number[] = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1];
 20  
 21  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 22  // 1) The old way, using `reduce()`: the result is not exact
 23  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 24  const sommeAvecReduce = nombres.reduce((accumulateur, valeur) => accumulateur + valeur, 0);
 25  console.log("somme avec reduce =", sommeAvecReduce);
 26  // we expect exactly 1.9, but the result often contains extra decimal places
 27  // (e.g., 1.9000000000000001) due to rounding errors that accumulate with each addition
 28  
 29  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 30  // 2) Math.sumPrecise(): adds all numbers exactly
 31  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 32  // unlike a loop of successive additions, the algorithm used internally
 33  // prevents the accumulation of intermediate rounding errors
 34  if (typeof Math.sumPrecise === "function") {
 35    const sommePrécise = Math.sumPrecise(nombres);
 36    console.log("somme avec Math.sumPrecise =", sommePrécise);
 37  } else {
 38    // This prevents a sudden crash (TypeError) to keep things simple:
 39    // this message will remain displayed until your engine JavaScript has
 40    // implemented this feature, even though it’s already finalized in the spec
 41    console.log("Math.sumPrecise n'est pas encore disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript",
 42      "(voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier)");
 43  }
 44  
 45  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 46  // Why is this useful? Financial, accounting, and scientific calculations—
 47  // anywhere where a small, repeated rounding error can become a real bug
 48  // (e.g., an invoice total that never comes out exactly to the cent)
 49  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/01-math-sumPrecise.ts

  1  somme avec reduce = 1.9000000000000004
  2  Math.sumPrecise n'est pas encore disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript (voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier)

docs.title: 16.3. script [02-iterator-concat]
docs.text:
[Iterator.concat] concatenates multiple iterables (array, Set, generator, etc.) into a single lazy iterator: the elements are generated only as needed, without constructing a complete intermediate collection—unlike the spread operator [...a, ...b], which copies everything immediately into memory.

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Iterator.concat()
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [Node 26+ - officially listed in the release notes for Node 26.0.0:
  6  // see https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0 - so it should already be
  7  // available if you're on Node 26. If not, check with:
  8  //   node -e "console.log(typeof Iterator.concat)"
  9  // See also ecmascript-2026/README.md for other new features in
 10  // this document, not all of which have the same level of availability]
 11  
 12  // Sometimes there are multiple data sources to iterate through one after another
 13  // (for example: multiple arrays, or an array followed by a Set, etc.)
 14  const premièreVague: string[] = ["Ana", "Léo"];
 15  const deuxièmeVague: Set<string> = new Set(["Nora", "Théo"]);
 16  const troisièmeVague: string[] = ["Zoé"];
 17  
 18  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 19  // 1) The old way: you had to group everything into a new array
 20  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 21  const tousLesInvitésTableau: string[] = [...premièreVague, ...deuxièmeVague, ...troisièmeVague];
 22  console.log("avec spread :", tousLesInvitésTableau);
 23  // Drawback: this creates a new array EN MÉMOIRE with all the elements copied over,
 24  // even if you only need the first two (e.g., for a paginated display)
 25  
 26  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 27  // 2) Iterator.concat(): concatenates iterables without copying them first
 28  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 29  // Iterator.concat accepts any type of iterable (array, Set, Map, generator, etc.)
 30  // and returns a "lazy" iterator: elements are generated only as needed
 31  if (typeof Iterator.concat === "function") {
 32    const tousLesInvités = Iterator.concat(premièreVague, deuxièmeVague, troisièmeVague);
 33  
 34    console.log("-----------------------");
 35    for (const invité of tousLesInvités) {
 36      console.log("invité =", invité);
 37    }
 38  
 39    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 40    // Advantage of "laziness": you can stop partway through
 41    // without having to pay the cost of building a complete collection in advance
 42    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 43    const troisPremiers = Iterator.concat(premièreVague, deuxièmeVague, troisièmeVague)
 44      .take(3)
 45      .toArray();
 46    console.log("trois premiers invités =", troisPremiers);
 47  } else {
 48    console.log("Iterator.concat n'est pas disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript",
 49      "(voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier)");
 50  }

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/02-iterator-concat.ts

  1  avec spread : [ 'Ana', 'Léo', 'Nora', 'Théo', 'Zoé' ]
  2  Iterator.concat n'est pas disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript (voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier)

docs.title: 16.4. script [03-error-isError]
docs.text:
[Error.isError] reliably detects whether a value is an error, even when it comes from another "realm" JavaScript (an isolated execution context—an iframe, a worker, or Node.js's vm module): Each realm has its own Error class, which causes <span style="color: #9a3412">instanceof Error to fail, as the script demonstrates in practice:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Error.isError()
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [Check availability yourself: see ecmascript-2026/README.md.
  6  // Some new features from ES2026 (such as Math.sumPrecise) are still missing
  7  // in V8 despite having reached Stage 4—it’s possible that this is also the case
  8  // here. Check with: node -e "console.log(typeof Error.isError)"]
  9  
 10  // Up until now, to determine if a value was an error, we used [instanceof Error]
 11  // (see exceptions/excep-03.ts) — this works well... except in certain tricky cases
 12  
 13  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 14  // 1) The pitfall of [instanceof] with multiple "realms" JavaScript
 15  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16  // A “realm” is an isolated execution context JavaScript: for example,
 17  // an iframe in a browser, a worker, or the Node.js module [vm] that allows
 18  // executing code in a separate context. Each realm has SA PROPRE class [Error],
 19  // distinct from that of the main realm.
 20  import vm from 'node:vm';
 21  
 22  // "new Error('from elsewhere')" is executed in a separate realm
 23  const erreurDunAutreRoyaume: unknown = vm.runInNewContext("new Error('venue d\\'ailleurs')");
 24  
 25  console.log("erreurDunAutreRoyaume =", erreurDunAutreRoyaume);
 26  // [instanceof Error] fails here: it is not PAS the same class [Error] as ours,
 27  // even though the object EST is, conceptually, an error
 28  console.log("erreurDunAutreRoyaume instanceof Error :", erreurDunAutreRoyaume instanceof Error);
 29  
 30  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 31  // 2) Error.isError(): reliable detection, even across different realms
 32  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 33  if (typeof Error.isError === "function") {
 34    console.log("Error.isError(erreurDunAutreRoyaume) :", Error.isError(erreurDunAutreRoyaume));
 35  
 36    // For comparison, for a “normal” error (same realm), both methods
 37    // yield the same result
 38    const erreurNormale = new Error("erreur classique");
 39    console.log("erreurNormale instanceof Error :", erreurNormale instanceof Error);
 40    console.log("Error.isError(erreurNormale) :", Error.isError(erreurNormale));
 41  
 42    // and a value that is clearly not an error
 43    console.log("Error.isError('abc') :", Error.isError("abc"));
 44    console.log("Error.isError(null) :", Error.isError(null));
 45  } else {
 46    console.log("Error.isError n'est pas disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript",
 47      "(voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier) - mais le piège avec [instanceof]",
 48      "démontré ci-dessus, lui, est bien réel et déjà observable");
 49  }

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/03-error-isError.ts

Execution result:

  1  erreurDunAutreRoyaume = Error: venue d'ailleurs
  2      at evalmachine.<anonymous>:1:1
  3  erreurDunAutreRoyaume instanceof Error : false
  4  Error.isError n'est pas disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript (voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier) - mais le piège avec [instanceof] démontré ci-dessus, lui, est bien réel et déjà observable

This script illustrates an interesting point even without Error.isError available: the line <span style="color: #9a3412">erreurDunAutreRoyaume instanceof Error: false clearly shows the actual pitfall that Error.isError is supposed to resolve—yet the object is, conceptually, a true error.

docs.title: 16.5. script [04-map-weakmap-getOrInsert]
docs.text:
[Map.prototype.getOrInsert]/[getOrInsertComputed] address a very common need: “if the key already exists, take its value; otherwise, create a default value and store it,” all in a single line rather than a verbose if (!map.has(key)) { map.set(...) }</span>. The same principle applies to WeakMap. 

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Map.prototype.getOrInsert / getOrInsertComputed
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [Node 26+ - officially listed in the release notes for Node 26.0.0:
  6  // see https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0 - so it should already be
  7  // available if you're on Node 26. If not, check with:
  8  //   node -e "console.log(typeof Map.prototype.getOrInsert)"
  9  // See also ecmascript-2026/README.md for other new features in
 10  // this document, which do not all have the same level of availability]
 11  
 12  // a very common requirement: "if the key already exists in the Map, take its value;
 13  // otherwise, create a default value, store it, then use it"
 14  
 15  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16  // 1) the old way: if/has() followed by set()—verbose and easy to write incorrectly
 17  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 18  const inscriptionsParAtelier = new Map<string, string[]>();
 19  
 20  function inscrireAncienneFaçon(atelier: string, participant: string): void {
 21    if (!inscriptionsParAtelier.has(atelier)) {
 22      inscriptionsParAtelier.set(atelier, []);
 23    }
 24    inscriptionsParAtelier.get(atelier)!.push(participant);
 25    // The "!" is necessary here: TypeScript cannot know, at this specific point,
 26    // that the .get() following a .set() just before it will necessarily succeed
 27  }
 28  inscrireAncienneFaçon("cuisine", "Ana");
 29  inscrireAncienneFaçon("cuisine", "Léo");
 30  console.log("avec l'ancienne façon :", inscriptionsParAtelier);
 31  
 32  if (typeof Map.prototype.getOrInsert !== "function") {
 33    console.log("Map.prototype.getOrInsert n'est pas disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript",
 34      "(voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier) - seule la partie 1) ci-dessus a pu s'exécuter");
 35  } else {
 36    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 37    // 2) Map.prototype.getOrInsert(): the same thing, in a single line
 38    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 39    const inscriptions2 = new Map<string, string[]>();
 40  
 41    const inscrire = (atelier: string, participant: string): void => {
 42      // returns the existing array for [atelier], or initializes it to [] if it does not yet exist
 43      inscriptions2.getOrInsert(atelier, []).push(participant);
 44    }
 45    inscrire("poterie", "Nora");
 46    inscrire("poterie", "Théo");
 47    console.log("avec getOrInsert :", inscriptions2);
 48  
 49    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 50    // 3) getOrInsertComputed(): the default value is calculated as QUE if necessary
 51    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 52    // with getOrInsert(key, value), the default [valeur] is evaluated as TOUJOURS,
 53    // even when the key already exists and isn’t needed (here it isn’t
 54    // a big deal for an empty array [], but it can be for a computationally expensive operation)
 55    const compteurs = new Map<string, number>();
 56  
 57    const incrémenter = (clé: string): void => {
 58      // the callback is not called QUE if the key does not yet exist in the Map
 59      const valeur = compteurs.getOrInsertComputed(clé, () => {
 60        console.log(`[calcul de la valeur initiale pour "${clé}"]`);
 61        return 0;
 62      });
 63      compteurs.set(clé, valeur + 1);
 64    }
 65    incrémenter("visites");
 66    incrémenter("visites"); // here, the callback will not be PAS re-executed
 67    incrémenter("clics");
 68    console.log("compteurs =", compteurs);
 69  
 70    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 71    // 4) WeakMap.prototype.getOrInsert / getOrInsertComputed: same principle,
 72    // to associate additional data with objects without preventing their
 73    // from being cleaned up by the garbage collector
 74    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 75    interface Métadonnées {
 76      vues: number;
 77    }
 78    const métadonnéesParObjet = new WeakMap<object, Métadonnées>();
 79  
 80    const enregistrerUneVue = (objet: object): void => {
 81      const métadonnées = métadonnéesParObjet.getOrInsertComputed(objet, () => ({ vues: 0 }));
 82      métadonnées.vues++;
 83    }
 84    const article = { titre: "Découverte du WeakMap" };
 85    enregistrerUneVue(article);
 86    enregistrerUneVue(article);
 87    console.log("métadonnées de l'article =", métadonnéesParObjet.get(article));
 88  }

docs.title: 16.6. script [05-uint8array-base64-hex]
docs.text:
Uint8Array (a raw byte array) now includes new methods for converting to and from Base64 and hexadecimal—formats commonly used to transmit binary data in JSON or URL—without relying on a third-party package:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Uint8Array: Base64 and hexadecimal conversion
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [Check availability yourself: see ecmascript-2026/README.md.
  6  // Some new features of ES2026 (such as Math.sumPrecise) are still missing
  7  // from V8 despite having reached Stage 4—it’s possible that this is also the case
  8  // here. Check with: node -e "console.log(typeof Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64)"]
  9  
 10  // [Uint8Array] is a typed array that stores raw bytes (values 0–255)—
 11  // for example, the contents of a file, an image, or data received over the network
 12  
 13  // before 2026, to encode these bytes in Base64 (the format used, for example,
 14  // in “data:” data streams, or to transmit binary data in JSON),
 15  // you had to use workarounds or third-party packages (Node.js-side buffers,
 16  // browser-side btoa/atob—which are imperfect and not originally designed for this purpose)
 17  
 18  const octets = new Uint8Array([72, 101, 108, 108, 111]); // "Hello" in ASCII codes
 19  
 20  if (typeof octets.toBase64 !== "function") {
 21    console.log("Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64 n'est pas disponible sur ce moteur JavaScript",
 22      "(voir le commentaire en tête de ce fichier)");
 23  } else {
 24    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 25    // 1) Base64 encoding
 26    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 27    const enBase64 = octets.toBase64();
 28    console.log("octets en base64 =", enBase64);
 29  
 30    // decoding: reconstructing a Uint8Array from a Base64 string
 31    const octetsRetrouvés = Uint8Array.fromBase64(enBase64);
 32    console.log("octets retrouvés =", octetsRetrouvés);
 33    console.log("identiques à l'original :", octets.toString() === octetsRetrouvés.toString());
 34  
 35    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 36    // 2) Hexadecimal encoding
 37    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 38    const enHexadécimal = octets.toHex();
 39    console.log("octets en hexadécimal =", enHexadécimal);
 40  
 41    const octetsDepuisHex = Uint8Array.fromHex(enHexadécimal);
 42    console.log("octets depuis hex =", octetsDepuisHex);
 43  
 44    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 45    // 3) Fill an existing Uint8Array starting at a given offset
 46    // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 47    // Useful for assembling multiple pieces into a single buffer without memory allocations
 48    // intermediate
 49    const buffer = new Uint8Array(10);
 50    const résultatEcriture = buffer.setFromHex("48656c6c6f"); // "Hello" in hexadecimal
 51    console.log("buffer après setFromHex =", buffer);
 52    console.log("caractères lus / écrits =", résultatEcriture);
 53  }
 54  
 55  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 56  // Why this is useful: transmitting binary data in text formats
 57  // (JSON, URL, HTTP headers...), without relying on a third-party package or workarounds
 58  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------

docs.title: 16.7. script [06-json-rawJSON-et-reviver]
docs.text:
This last script differs from the previous ones: [JSON.rawJSON]/[isRawJSON], as well as the new "context" parameter in the JSON.parse reviver, already work in the preparation environment for this course (Node 22):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] JSON.rawJSON / JSON.isRawJSON, and the context of reviver
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [these two new features already work with Node 22, unlike the other
  6  // scripts in this folder, which require Node 24—see ecmascript-2026/README.md]
  7  
  8  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  9  // 1) The problem: JSON.stringify loses precision with large integers
 10  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11  // A standard JavaScript number (of type [number]) cannot be represented
 12  // exactly represent integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (see bases/bases-09.ts)
 13  // However, many API (databases, social media, etc.) do send
 14  // 17- to 19-digit numerical identifiers in their JSON
 15  const identifiantColonneBaseDeDonnées = "9007199254740993123"; // which is too long for a [number]
 16  
 17  interface Enregistrement {
 18    id: unknown; // unknown here because it will be either a RawJSON or a normal value
 19    nom: string;
 20  }
 21  
 22  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 23  // 2) JSON.rawJSON(): inserts a "raw" number into a JSON.stringify,
 24  //    without ever converting it to the type [number] (thus without any loss of precision)
 25  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 26  const enregistrement: Enregistrement = {
 27    id: JSON.rawJSON(identifiantColonneBaseDeDonnées),
 28    nom: "capteur-température-3"
 29  };
 30  
 31  const texteJSON = JSON.stringify(enregistrement);
 32  console.log("texteJSON =", texteJSON);
 33  // the identifier appears exactly as is in the generated text, digit by digit,
 34  // whereas an ID of the form: Number(identifiantColonneBaseDeDonnées) would have been rounded
 35  
 36  // JSON.isRawJSON() allows you to verify whether a value was created by JSON.rawJSON
 37  console.log("JSON.isRawJSON(enregistrement.id) =", JSON.isRawJSON(enregistrement.id));
 38  
 39  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 40  // 3) The reviver for JSON.parse now accepts a third parameter, [context]
 41  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 42  // Before 2026, the reviver only accepted (key, value): impossible to know
 43  // what the text was—JSON EXACT—or where this value came from (which is actually useful
 44  // to retrieve a large number without loss, by keeping it in text form)
 45  const objetRelu = JSON.parse(texteJSON, (clé, valeur, context) => {
 46    // [context.source] returns the raw text JSON corresponding to this value,
 47    // before any conversion to the type JavaScript—undefined for objects/arrays
 48    if (context?.source !== undefined) {
 49      console.log(`clé="${clé}", valeur convertie=${valeur}, texte JSON d'origine="${context.source}"`);
 50    }
 51    return valeur;
 52  });
 53  console.log("objetRelu =", objetRelu);
  • [JSON.rawJSON(texte)] inserts a "raw" number into JSON.stringify without ever converting it to the number type—useful for very large numeric identifiers (beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, see bases-09), which would otherwise lose precision;
  • the third parameter, context, of the reviver function provides access, via context.source</span>, to the raw text JSON of the value currently being processed—before any conversion to the JavaScript type. 
    npx tsx ecmascript-2026/06-json-rawJSON-et-reviver.ts

    Execution result:

      1  texteJSON = {"id":9007199254740993123,"nom":"capteur-température-3"}
  2  JSON.isRawJSON(enregistrement.id) = true
  3  clé="id", valeur convertie=9007199254740993000, texte JSON d'origine="9007199254740993123"
  4  clé="nom", valeur convertie=capteur-température-3, texte JSON d'origine=""capteur-température-3""
  5  objetRelu = { id: 9007199254740993000, nom: 'capteur-température-3' }

    We can clearly see the benefit of JSON.rawJSON: the text generated by JSON preserves the identifier digit by digit (9007199254740993123), whereas a simple id: Number(...) would have rounded it—as demonstrated by the value returned by JSON.parse (9007199254740993000), which was indeed converted to the number type and lost precision.

docs.title: 7. Regular Expressions
docs.text: The scripts in this chapter are located in the [regexp] folder of the project. In both TypeScript and JavaScript, a regular expression is not a string but a separate object of type RegExp—therefore, you do not enclose a regular expression in quotes.

docs.title: 7.1. script [regexp-01]
docs.text:
This script matches several strings against different patterns (a sequence of digits, a dd/mm/yy date, a decimal number) and retrieves the captured groups:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  /// regular expressions in JavaScript
  4  // extract the various fields from a string
  5  // The pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
  6  // we only want to extract the sequence of digits
  7  let modèle: RegExp = /(\d+)/;
  8  console.log("type d'une expression régulière : ", typeof (modèle));
  9  // We compare the string to the pattern
 10  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
 11  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "12 34");
 12  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "abcd");
 13  
 14  // The pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
 15  // We want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that come before and after it
 16  modèle = /^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/;
 17  // We match the string against the pattern
 18  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
 19  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "12 34");
 20  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "abcd");
 21  
 22  // the pattern: a date in dd/mm/yy format
 23  modèle = /^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/;
 24  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "10/05/97");
 25  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "  04/04/01  ");
 26  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "5/1/01");
 27  
 28  // the pattern—a decimal number
 29  modèle = /^\s*([+|-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*$/;
 30  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "187.8");
 31  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "-0.6");
 32  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "4");
 33  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, ".6");
 34  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "4.");
 35  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, " + 4");
 36  
 37  // --------------------------------------------------------------------------
 38  function compareModèleToChaîne(modèle: RegExp, chaîne: string): void {
 39    // compares the string [chaîne] to the pattern [modèle]
 40    console.log(`----------- chaîne=${chaîne}, modèle=${modèle}`)
 41    // the string is compared to the pattern
 42    const result1 = modèle.exec(chaîne);
 43    console.log(`comparaison avec exec=`, result1);
 44    // another way to do it
 45    const result2 = chaîne.match(modèle);
 46    console.log(`comparaison avec match=`, result2);
 47  }
  • line 7: let model: RegExp = /(\d+)/ — the type RegExp is explicit here, but TypeScript would have deduced it automatically from the syntax /.../ anyway;
  • The methods [modèle.exec(chaîne)] and [chaîne.match(modèle)] return the same result: either null (no match) or an array where:
    • the element [0] is the entire string that matches the pattern;
    • the elements [1], [2]... correspond to the groups captured in parentheses, in order;
    • the .index property returns the position of the match within the string;
    • the .input property returns the original string.

docs.title: 7.2. script [regexp-02]
docs.text:
Sometimes, you don’t want to extract elements from the string being tested—you just want to know if it matches the pattern. In that case, use [RegExp.test] instead of exec/match, and you can remove the capture parentheses, which are no longer needed:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  /// regular expressions in JavaScript
  4  // Extracting the different fields from a string
  5  // The pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
  6  // We only want to extract the sequence of digits
  7  let modèle: RegExp = /\d+/;
  8  console.log("type d'une expression régulière : ", typeof (modèle));
  9  // We match the string against the pattern
 10  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
 11  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "12 34");
 12  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "abcd");
 13  
 14  // The pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
 15  // We want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that come before and after it
 16  modèle = /^.*?\d+.*?$/;
 17  // We match the string against the pattern
 18  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
 19  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "12 34");
 20  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "abcd");
 21  
 22  // the pattern: a date in dd/mm/yy format
 23  modèle = /^\s*\d\d\/\d\d\/\d\d\s*$/;
 24  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "10/05/97");
 25  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "  04/04/01  ");
 26  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "5/1/01");
 27  
 28  // the pattern—a decimal number
 29  modèle = /^\s*[+|-]?\s*\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+\s*$/;
 30  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "187.8");
 31  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "-0.6");
 32  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "4");
 33  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, ".6");
 34  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, "4.");
 35  compareModèleToChaîne(modèle, " + 4");
 36  
 37  // --------------------------------------------------------------------------
 38  function compareModèleToChaîne(modèle: RegExp, chaîne: string): void {
 39    // test
 40    const correspond = modèle.test(chaîne);
 41    // compares the string [chaîne] to the pattern [modèle]
 42    console.log(`----------- chaîne=${chaîne}, modèle=${modèle}, correspond=${correspond}`);
 43  }
