docs.title: 2. Setting Up a Development Environment
docs.text:
The original document (2019) provided detailed instructions for installing [Laragon], [Netbeans], and [Visual Studio Code] on Windows 10, with numerous screenshots illustrating the configuration of PATH. In 2026, the installation is much simpler: we will use the following tools.

  • [Visual Studio Code] to generate the code TypeScript;
  • [Node.js], version 26 or later—this is the version that made the [Temporal] object, presented in the last chapter of this document, available without any special options;
  • [TypeScript], version 6;
  • [tsx], a tool that runs a .ts file directly without a prior compilation step—this is what we will use for all the scripts in this document;
  • [npm] (Node Package Manager), included with Node.js, to install the libraries we’ll need;
  • a PHP 7 server (see the course “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples”), required only for the final chapters of this document (the HTTP client for the tax calculation service). Its installation is described in the corresponding chapter.

docs.title: 2.2.2. The tsconfig.json file
docs.text:
This file configures the TypeScript compiler. Strict mode is enabled: this is the recommended configuration, as it allows TypeScript to detect as many errors as possible during compilation.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "lib": ["ESNext"],
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "strict": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["**/*.ts"]
}
Important: Starting with TypeScript 6.0, the "types" line: ["node"] is essential: without it, TypeScript no longer automatically recognizes the global objects of Node.js as a console or process, unlike versions prior to 6.0.

Next, install the dependencies listed in package.json:

npm install

docs.title: 2.3. First script
docs.text:
Let’s create a file named tests/test-01.ts:

// a first program TypeScript
console.log("hello world!");

Run it from the terminal, in the project root directory:

npx tsx tests/test-01.ts

Execution result:

  1  hello world!

docs.title: 2.4. Second script: type checking
docs.text:
Let’s create a second file, <span style="color: #9a3412">tests/test-02.ts, with an explicitly typed variable:

'use strict'
let x: number = 4;
console.log("x=", x);

npx tsx tests/test-02.ts

Execution result:

  1  x= 4

Now let's try assigning a string to this variable declared as a number:

x = "abc";

Without even running the script, VSCode immediately highlights the line in red, and the type-checking command fails:

npx tsc --noEmit

Execution result:

  1  tests/test-02.ts(4,1): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

This is the key advantage of TypeScript over JavaScript: an entire category of errors (accidentally mixing types) is detected before execution, directly in the editor, rather than discovered when the code crashes in production.

docs.title: 2.5. ESLint
docs.text:
[ESLint] is a tool that verifies that the code adheres to a set of style rules and best practices (unused variables, suspicious comparisons, etc.). The configuration file .eslintrc.cjs (the .cjs extension, not .js, is required because package.json declares "type": "module") uses the @typescript-eslint parser, which understands the TypeScript syntax (types, interfaces, private fields #x...):

module.exports = {
  root: true,
  env: { node: true, es2024: true },
  extends: ["eslint:recommended", "plugin:@typescript-eslint/recommended"],
  parser: "@typescript-eslint/parser",
  plugins: ["@typescript-eslint"],
  parserOptions: { ecmaVersion: "latest", sourceType: "module" }
};

We then analyze the entire project using:

npx eslint . --ext .ts

docs.title: 2.6. VSCode ESLint
docs.text:
The VSCode extension, named [ESLint] (to be installed from the Extensions tab), displays ESLint warnings directly in the editor in real time—without having to run the command manually each time.

We now have a complete working environment. The next chapter covers the basics of the TypeScript language.

docs.title: 6. Strings
docs.text: The scripts in this chapter are located in the [strings] folder of the project.

docs.title: 6.1. script [str-01]
docs.text:
The first thing to understand is that once a string is created, it can no longer be modified (it is immutable). There are many methods available to create a new string from the original string, but the original string always remains unchanged.

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // the strings are read-only (they cannot be modified)
  4  
  5  // a string
  6  const chaîne1: string = "abcd ";
  7  // type
  8  console.log("typeof(chaîne1)=", typeof (chaîne1));
  9  // character #2
 10  console.log("chaîne1[2]=", chaîne1[2]);
 11  // causes an error
 12  // [mise à jour TypeScript] TypeScript detects the error during compilation:
 13  // a string has read-only access by index
 14  // @ts-expect-error: a string is read-only
 15  chaîne1[2] = "0";
  • Line 10: string1[2] reads the third character of the string (index 0);
  • Line 15: string 1[2] = "0" attempts a write operation, which TypeScript rejects at compile time, thanks to @ts-expect-error—the comment above confirms that this error is expected and is intended precisely to demonstrate it.

Type checking:

npx tsc --noEmit

Execution result:

  1  strings/str-01.ts(15,1): error TS2540: Cannot assign to '2' because it is a read-only property.

Execution with tsx (without prior type checking):

npx tsx strings/str-01.ts

Execution result:

  1  typeof(chaîne1)= string
  2  chaîne1[2]= c
  3  TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property '2' of string 'abcd '
  4      at strings/str-01.ts:15:10

docs.title: 6.2. script [str-02]
docs.text:
A character string can be one of two types: [string] (literal string) or [object] (instance of the [String] class):

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // String literals can be of two types
  4  
  5  // a string literal
  6  const chaîne1: string = "abcd ";
  7  // type
  8  console.log("typeof(chaîne1)=", typeof (chaîne1));
  9  // String instance
 10  // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/ban-types -- here, [String] (object) is the exact type needed, not [string] (primitive): that is precisely the point of the demo
 11  const chaîne2: String = new String("xyzt");
 12  // type
 13  console.log("typeof(chaîne2)=", typeof (chaîne2));
 14  // alternative notation (without `new`)
 15  const chaîne3: string = String("12 34");
 16  // type
 17  console.log("typeof(chaîne3)=", typeof (chaîne3));
 18  // The type [string] and the type [object] offer the same methods—those of the String class
 19  console.log("chaîne1.length=", chaîne1.length);
 20  console.log("chaîne2.length=", chaîne2.length);
  • Line 6: the standard way to define a string—string1 will be of type string;
  • line 12: new String(...)</span> creates a string object—string2 will be of type object. Here, the declared type TypeScript is String (with a capital S), the *wrapper object* type, which is different from the primitive type string (lowercase);
  • both types offer the same methods—those of the String class.
    • npx tsx strings/str-02.ts

    Execution result:

      1  typeof(chaîne1)= string
  2  typeof(chaîne2)= object
  3  typeof(chaîne3)= string
  4  chaîne1.length= 5
  5  chaîne2.length= 4

docs.title: 6.3. script [str-03]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates variable interpolation in a string:

  1  'use strict';
  2  
  3  // string
  4  const chaîne: string = "Introduction à Javascript par l'exemple";
  5  // string with variable interpolation
  6  const str: string = `[${chaîne}].substr(3, 2)=` + chaîne.substr(3, 2)
  7  console.log(str);
  • Line 6: A string enclosed in backticks (*backticks*, AltGr-7 on a French keyboard) can contain ${variable} expressions, which are replaced by the variable’s value—this is called a template string.
npx tsx strings/str-03.ts

Result of execution:

  1  [Introduction à Javascript par l'exemple].substr(3, 2)=ro

docs.title: 6.4. script [str-04]
docs.text:
The template string alone is insufficient for precise formatting (width, alignment, decimal precision, etc.). For this purpose, we use an external package, [sprintf-js], which replicates the printf/sprintf functions familiar from other languages. It is installed with <span style="color: #9a3412">npm install sprintf-js</span> and can be easily imported:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // Using an external package to access the sprintf function
  3  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  4  // string
  5  const chaîne: string = "Introduction à Javascript par l'exemple";
  6  // method
  7  console.log(sprintf("[%s].substr(3,2)=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.substr(3, 2)));
Background: In 2019, the `import` statement caused issues with Node.js (which did not yet natively support modules, as seen in ECMAScript), and required an intermediate package called `esm`. This is no longer the case as of Node 12+: our project, with "type": "module" in package.json, uses import/export natively, without any additional configuration. 
npx tsx strings/str-04.ts

Execution result:

  1  [Introduction à Javascript par l'exemple].substr(3,2)=[ro]

docs.title: 6.5. script [str-05]
docs.text:
The [sprintf] function accepts, as in C, "formats" introduced by %: %s (string), %d (integer), %f (floating-point), %j (JSON), %T (type), %t (boolean), along with width and alignment modifiers (%20s, %-20s, %04d...):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // Using an external package to access the sprintf function
  3  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  4  // string
  5  const chaîne: string = "Javascript";
  6  // strings
  7  console.log(sprintf("[%s, %%s]=>[%s]", chaîne, chaîne));
  8  console.log(sprintf("[%s, %%20s]=>[%20s]", chaîne, chaîne));
  9  console.log(sprintf("[%s, %%-20s]=>[%-20s]", chaîne, chaîne));
 10  // integers
 11  console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%d]=>[%d]", 10, 10));
 12  console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%4d]=>[%4d]", 10, 10));
 13  console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%-4d]=>[%-4d]", 10, 10));
 14  console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%04d]=>[%04d]", 10, 10));
 15  // floating-point numbers
 16  console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%f]=>[%f]", -10.5, -10.5));
 17  console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%10.2f]=>[%10.2f]", -10.5, -10.5));
 18  console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%-10.2f]=>[%-10.2f]", -10.5, -10.5));
 19  console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%010.3f]=>[%010.3f]", -10.5, -10.5));
 20  // json
 21  console.log(sprintf("personne (%%j)=%j", { nom: "mathieu", âge: 34 }));
 22  // type
 23  console.log(sprintf("type personne (%%T)=%T", { nom: "mathieu", âge: 34 }));
 24  // boolean
 25  console.log(sprintf("booléen (%%t)=%t", 4 === 4));

npx tsx strings/str-05.ts

Execution result:

  1  [Javascript, %s]=>[Javascript]
  2  [Javascript, %20s]=>[          Javascript]
  3  [Javascript, %-20s]=>[Javascript          ]
  4  [10, %d]=>[10]
  5  [10, %4d]=>[  10]
  6  [10, %-4d]=>[10  ]
  7  [10, %04d]=>[0010]
  8  [-10.5, %f]=>[-10.5]
  9  [-10.5, %10.2f]=>[    -10.50]
 10  [-10.5, %-10.2f]=>[-10.50    ]
 11  [-10.5, %010.3f]=>[-00010.500]
 12  personne (%j)={"nom":"mathieu","âge":34}
 13  type personne (%T)=object
 14  booléen (%t)=true

docs.title: 6.6. [str-06] script
docs.text:
This script lists the most common methods of the [String] class:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // Using an external package to access the sprintf function
  3  import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
  4  // string
  5  const chaîne: string = "  Introduction à Javascript ";
  6  // a few methods
  7  // substr(10,2): 2 characters starting at position 10
  8  console.log(sprintf("[%s].substr(10,2)=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.substr(10, 2)));
  9  // trim: removes whitespace at the beginning and end of a string (whitespace = \b \t \r \n \f)
 10  console.log(sprintf("[%s].trim()=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.trim()));
 11  // toLowerCase: conversion to lowercase
 12  console.log(sprintf("[%s].toLowerCase=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.toLowerCase()));
 13  // toUpperCase: conversion to uppercase
 14  console.log(sprintf("[%s].toUpperCase=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.toUpperCase()));
 15  // indexOf: position of a searched string within the string; -1 if the substring does not exist
 16  console.log(sprintf("[%s].indexOf('Java')=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.indexOf('Java')));
 17  console.log(sprintf("[%s].trim().indexOf('abcd')=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.indexOf('abcd')));
 18  // includes: true if the searched string is in the string
 19  console.log(sprintf("[%s].includes('Java')=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.includes('Java')));
 20  // length: length of the string—this is not a method but a property
 21  console.log(sprintf("[%s].length=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.length));
 22  // slice (7,10): characters 7 through 9
 23  console.log(sprintf("[%s].slice(7,10)=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.slice(7, 10)));
 24  // match: searches for an expression in the string—this expression can be a regular expression
 25  // /intro/i: regular expression matching the string [intro] in either uppercase or lowercase
 26  // returns the found string
 27  console.log(sprintf("[%s].match(/intro/i)=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.match(/intro/i)));
 28  // replace: replaces string1 with string2 in string
 29  // replaces the first occurrence of i with x
 30  console.log(sprintf("[%s].replace('i','x')=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.replace('i', 'x')));
 31  // replaces all occurrences of i with x
 32  // /i/g is a regular expression that matches all (g) occurrences of i
 33  console.log(sprintf("[%s].replace(/i/g,'x')=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.replace(/i/g, 'x')));
 34  // split: splits the string into words separated by the split parameter
 35  // returns an array of these words
 36  // /\s*/: words separated by zero or more spaces
 37  console.log(sprintf("[%s].split(/\\s*/)=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.split(/\s*/)));
 38  // /\s+/: words separated by one or more spaces
 39  console.log(sprintf("[%s].split(/\\s+/)=[%s]", chaîne, chaîne.split(/\s+/)));
  • [trim] removes leading and trailing whitespace; [toLowerCase]/[toUpperCase] change the case;
  • [indexOf] returns the position of a substring (-1 if absent); [includes] returns a Boolean;
  • [slice] extracts a substring by position; [match] matches the string against a regular expression (see next chapter);
  • [replace] replaces the first occurrence found (or all occurrences, with a /g regex); [split] splits the string into an array of words.
npx tsx strings/str-06.ts

Execution result:

  1  [  Introduction à Javascript ].substr(10,2)=[ti]
  2  [  Introduction à Javascript ].trim()=[Introduction à Javascript]
  3  [  Introduction à Javascript ].toLowerCase=[  introduction à javascript ]
  4  [  Introduction à Javascript ].toUpperCase=[  INTRODUCTION À JAVASCRIPT ]
  5  [  Introduction à Javascript ].indexOf('Java')=[17]
  6  [  Introduction à Javascript ].trim().indexOf('abcd')=[-1]
  7  [  Introduction à Javascript ].includes('Java')=[true]
  8  [  Introduction à Javascript ].length=[28]
  9  [  Introduction à Javascript ].slice(7,10)=[duc]
 10  [  Introduction à Javascript ].match(/intro/i)=[Intro]
 11  [  Introduction à Javascript ].replace('i','x')=[  Introductxon à Javascript ]
 12  [  Introduction à Javascript ].replace(/i/g,'x')=[  Introductxon à Javascrxpt ]
 13  [  Introduction à Javascript ].split(/\s*/)=[,I,n,t,r,o,d,u,c,t,i,o,n,à,J,a,v,a,s,c,r,i,p,t,]
 14  [  Introduction à Javascript ].split(/\s+/)=[,Introduction,à,Javascript,]

docs.title: 6.7. script [str-07]
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] Three new features introduced between 2020 and 2024: [replaceAll], [matchAll], and the detection/correction of “malformed” strings:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] new string methods
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7  // 1) replaceAll (search, replace)  (ECMAScript 2021)
  8  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  9  // str-06.js shows that replace() with a string only replaces the first occurrence
 10  // and that a regular expression with /i/g was needed to replace everything
 11  const chaîne: string = "un chat, deux chats, trois chats";
 12  console.log("replace (1 seule occurrence) :", chaîne.replace("chat", "chien"));
 13  console.log("replaceAll (toutes les occurrences) :", chaîne.replaceAll("chat", "chien"));
 14  // replaceAll also accepts a regular expression, but it must have the flag [g]
 15  console.log("replaceAll avec regexp :", chaîne.replaceAll(/chat/g, "chien"));
 16  
 17  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 18  // 2) matchAll(regexp)  (ECMAScript 2020)
 19  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 20  // `match()` with the `[g]` flag returns only the matched strings, without their positions or groups
 21  // matchAll() returns an iterator that provides, for each occurrence, all the information (like exec())
 22  const texte: string = "Jean a 30 ans, Marie a 25 ans, Paul a 40 ans";
 23  const modèle: RegExp = /(\w+) a (\d+) ans/g;
 24  
 25  // With `match` (flag `g`): the details of the captured groups are lost
 26  console.log("match =", texte.match(modèle));
 27  
 28  // with matchAll: the details are retained (captured name, captured age, position...)
 29  console.log("-----------------------");
 30  for (const résultat of texte.matchAll(modèle)) {
 31    console.log("nom =", résultat[1], ", âge =", résultat[2], ", position =", résultat.index);
 32  }
 33  
 34  // You can also convert the iterator into an array using the spread operator
 35  const tousLesRésultats = [...texte.matchAll(modèle)];
 36  console.log("nombre de correspondances =", tousLesRésultats.length);
 37  
 38  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 39  // 3) isWellFormed() / toWellFormed()  (ECMAScript 2024)
 40  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 41  // A string JavaScript may contain an isolated invalid "half-Unicode character"
 42  // (for example, when a string has been improperly split). This can cause
 43  // certain functions (encodeURIComponent, ...)
 44  const chaîneValide: string = "café ☕";
 45  const chaîneMalFormée: string = "abc\uD800def"; // \uD800 is an isolated “half-character” that is invalid on its own
 46  
 47  console.log("chaîneValide.isWellFormed() =", chaîneValide.isWellFormed());
 48  console.log("chaîneMalFormée.isWellFormed() =", chaîneMalFormée.isWellFormed());
 49  
 50  // toWellFormed() replaces invalid characters with the replacement character �
 51  console.log("chaîneMalFormée.toWellFormed() =", chaîneMalFormée.toWellFormed());
  • [replaceAll] (ES2021) replaces all occurrences of a string without requiring a /g regular expression, as in the str-06 script;
  • [matchAll] (ES2020) returns an iterator of all results found, each with its captured groups ET and its position—whereas <span style="color: #9a3412">match with the g flag returns only the found strings, without this detail;
  • [isWellFormed]/[toWellFormed] (ES2024) detects and corrects strings containing an isolated “half Unicode character” (often caused by incorrect string splitting), which can cause certain functions—such as encodeURIComponent—to crash.
npx tsx strings/str-07.ts

Execution result:

  1  replace (1 seule occurrence) : un chien, deux chats, trois chats
  2  replaceAll (toutes les occurrences) : un chien, deux chiens, trois chiens
  3  replaceAll avec regexp : un chien, deux chiens, trois chiens
  4  match = [ 'Jean a 30 ans', 'Marie a 25 ans', 'Paul a 40 ans' ]
  5  -----------------------
  6  nom = Jean , âge = 30 , position = 0
  7  nom = Marie , âge = 25 , position = 15
  8  nom = Paul , âge = 40 , position = 31
  9  nombre de correspondances = 3
 10  chaîneValide.isWellFormed() = true
 11  chaîneMalFormée.isWellFormed() = false
 12  chaîneMalFormée.toWellFormed() = abc�def

docs.title: 17. Temporal: the modern replacement for Date
docs.text: [Temporal] is a new global namespace intended to replace the old Date object, which has long been considered flawed: mutability, months numbered 0 through 11, lack of true time zone handling, and ambiguous string parsing. Date has not been removed from the language—existing code continues to work—but Temporal is now the recommended approach for any new code that manipulates dates, times, and durations.

docs.title: 17.1. ⚠️ Exact status regarding ECMAScript 2026
docs.text: The Temporal proposal reached Stage 4 of TC39 in March 2026, and numerous articles have presented it as part of ECMAScript 2026. However, the official section of the specification summarizing the content of ECMAScript 2026 (cited in the previous chapter) does not explicitly mention it—the matter remains to be clarified. In practical terms, Temporal is natively available in Node.js 26 and up-to-date browsers, making this chapter relevant right now.

docs.title: 17.2. ⚠️ “Homemade” TypeScript
docs.text: As with the previous chapter, TypeScript does not yet natively support the Temporal API in its standard type files. The project’s temporal/types-temporal.d.ts file manually declares only the members actually used in the scripts in this chapter—not the entire, very extensive API.

docs.title: 17.3. [01-plainDate-plainTime-plainDateTime] script
docs.text:
This script presents [Temporal.PlainDate] (a date without time or time zone), [Temporal.PlainTime] (a time without date), and [Temporal.PlainDateTime] (date + time, without time zone):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Temporal: PlainDate, PlainTime, PlainDateTime
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [nécessite Node 26+ - voir temporal/README.md]
  6  
  7  // [Temporal] is a brand-new namespace, designed to replace [Date],
  8  //, which had several flaws: mutability, months numbered from 0 to 11
  9  // (January = 0!), lack of true time zone support, and a
 10  // single object intended to represent both a date, a time ET, and a specific moment.
 11  // Temporal clearly separates these concepts into several types.
 12  
 13  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 14  // 1) Temporal.PlainDate: a date SANS with no time or time zone
 15  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16  // Useful for: a birthday, a due date, a holiday...
 17  // concepts that do not have a “specific time of day”
 18  const anniversaire = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-08-24");
 19  console.log("anniversaire =", anniversaire.toString());
 20  console.log("année =", anniversaire.year, ", mois =", anniversaire.month, ", jour =", anniversaire.day);
 21  // Unlike the old Date class, the month is numbered normally: 8 = August (not 7!)
 22  console.log("jour de la semaine (1=lundi..7=dimanche) =", anniversaire.dayOfWeek);
 23  console.log("nombre de jours dans ce mois =", anniversaire.daysInMonth);
 24  
 25  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 26  // 2) Immutability: add() and subtract() return a NOUVEL object
 27  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 28  // With the old `Date`, `date.setDate(date.getDate()) + 7` modifies the existing object—
 29  // a common source of bugs when this object is shared elsewhere in the code
 30  const dansUneSemaine = anniversaire.add({ days: 7 });
 31  console.log("anniversaire (inchangé) =", anniversaire.toString());
 32  console.log("dansUneSemaine (nouvel objet) =", dansUneSemaine.toString());
 33  
 34  // month arithmetic: automatically handles the number of days in the following month
 35  const finJanvier = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-01-31");
 36  const unMoisPlusTard = finJanvier.add({ months: 1 });
 37  console.log("finJanvier =", finJanvier.toString(), ", +1 mois =", unMoisPlusTard.toString());
 38  // -> "2026-02-28" and not a strange overflow in March, unlike the old Date
 39  
 40  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 41  // 3) comparison of two dates
 42  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 43  const rentrée = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-09-01");
 44  console.log("anniversaire avant rentrée :", Temporal.PlainDate.compare(anniversaire, rentrée) < 0);
 45  console.log("égalité :", anniversaire.equals("2026-08-24"));
 46  
 47  // duration between two dates
 48  const durée = anniversaire.until(rentrée);
 49  console.log("durée jusqu'à la rentrée =", durée.toString());
 50  
 51  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 52  // 4) Temporal.PlainTime: a time SANS with no date or time zone
 53  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 54  // Useful for: “The class starts at 2:30 p.m.,” regardless of the day
 55  const heureDeCours = Temporal.PlainTime.from("14:30:00");
 56  console.log("heureDeCours =", heureDeCours.toString());
 57  const finDeCours = heureDeCours.add({ hours: 1, minutes: 30 });
 58  console.log("finDeCours =", finDeCours.toString());
 59  
 60  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 61  // 5) Temporal.PlainDateTime: date + time, but SANS time zone
 62  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 63  // Useful for: a "general" appointment without worrying about the time zone (e.g., a form
 64  // that simply displays “August 24, 2026, 2:30 PM” without specifying a location)
 65  const rendezVous = Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2026-08-24T14:30:00");
 66  console.log("rendezVous =", rendezVous.toString());
 67  // you can extract the date and time parts separately
 68  console.log("partie date =", rendezVous.toPlainDate().toString());
 69  console.log("partie heure =", rendezVous.toPlainTime().toString());
  • Unlike the old Date, the month in Temporal.PlainDate is numbered normally: 8 refers to August, not July;
  • [immutabilité]: add() and subtract() always return a new object—the original is never modified, unlike in Date.prototype.setDate;
  • Arithmetic operations on months automatically handle different month lengths (January 31 + 1 month correctly yields February 28, not an overflow into March);
  • Temporal.PlainDate.compare(...) and .until(...) allow you to compare two dates and calculate the duration between them.

docs.title: 17.4. script [02-zonedDateTime]
docs.text:
[Temporal.ZonedDateTime] is the type closest to the old Date: it combines date, time, and time zone in a reliable and explicit way:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Temporal.ZonedDateTime: the true replacement for Date
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [nécessite Node 26+ - voir temporal/README.md]
  6  
  7  // [Temporal.ZonedDateTime] is the closest equivalent to the old [Date]:
  8  // It combines a date, a time (ET), and a time zone—but does so reliably
  9  // and explicitly, whereas [Date] handled this in a confusing and implicit way.
 10  
 11  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 12  // 1) creation of a ZonedDateTime, with a time zone EXPLICITE
 13  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 14  // unlike "new Date('2026-08-24T14:30:00')", which is ambiguous (local time?
 15  // UTC? It depends on the format and the engine JS!), here the time zone is required
 16  const réunionParis = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-08-24T14:30:00[Europe/Paris]");
 17  console.log("réunionParis =", réunionParis.toString());
 18  console.log("fuseau =", réunionParis.timeZoneId, ", décalage =", réunionParis.offset);
 19  
 20  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 21  // 2) Convert the same meeting to a different time zone
 22  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 23  // withTimeZone() does not change PAS the actual time, only the way it is displayed—
 24  // useful for showing the time of the same event to participants around the world
 25  const réunionNewYork = réunionParis.withTimeZone("America/New_York");
 26  console.log("même réunion, vue depuis New York =", réunionNewYork.toString());
 27  const réunionTokyo = réunionParis.withTimeZone("Asia/Tokyo");
 28  console.log("même réunion, vue depuis Tokyo =", réunionTokyo.toString());
 29  
 30  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 31  // 3) The calculations automatically handle daylight saving time changes (DST)
 32  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 33  // This is the classic pitfall of the old Date function: adding "24 hours" doesn't match
 34  // Always add "1 day" during a daylight saving time change
 35  const avantChangementHeure = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-10-24T20:00:00[Europe/Paris]");
 36  // Add one “calendar” day: Temporal understands that the time change must be skipped
 37  const unJourPlusTard = avantChangementHeure.add({ days: 1 });
 38  console.log("avant =", avantChangementHeure.toString());
 39  console.log("+ 1 jour calendaire =", unJourPlusTard.toString());
 40  // exactly 24 hours are added: this is not PAS necessarily the same local time
 41  // if a daylight saving time change has occurred in the meantime
 42  const vingtQuatreHeuresPlusTard = avantChangementHeure.add({ hours: 24 });
 43  console.log("+ 24 heures exactement =", vingtQuatreHeuresPlusTard.toString());
 44  
 45  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 46  // 4) the current time, in the system’s time zone
 47  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 48  const maintenant = Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO();
 49  console.log("maintenant =", maintenant.toString());
 50  console.log("fuseau du système =", Temporal.Now.timeZoneId());
 51  
 52  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 53  // 5) Comparison and duration between two ZonedDateTime in different time zones
 54  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 55  const départAvion = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-12-20T22:00:00[Europe/Paris]");
 56  const arrivéeAvion = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-12-21T11:30:00[Asia/Tokyo]");
 57  // Temporal compares the actual times, regardless of the time zone displayed on each side
 58  const duréeVol = départAvion.until(arrivéeAvion);
 59  console.log("durée du vol =", duréeVol.toString());
  • unlike new Date('2026-08-24T14:30:00'), whose interpretation (local time or UTC) depends on the exact format of the string, Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(...) requires an explicit time zone, enclosed in square brackets;
  • withTimeZone(...) converts the display of the same actual time to another time zone, without changing the time itself—useful for displaying a meeting time to participants in multiple countries;
  • the arithmetic correctly handles daylight saving time changes: adding “1 calendar day” is not always the same as adding “exactly 24 hours”—a classic pitfall of the old Date function.

docs.title: 17.5. script [03-duration-et-instant]
docs.text:
[Temporal.Duration] represents a period of time (not a specific moment); [Temporal.Instant] represents a specific, universal point in time—the direct replacement for new Date(...).getTime():

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Temporal.Duration and Temporal.Instant
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [nécessite Node 26+ - voir temporal/README.md]
  6  
  7  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  8  // 1) Temporal.Duration: represents a LAPS of time (not a specific moment)
  9  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 10  // Previously, a duration had to be cobbled together “by hand” in milliseconds—
 11  // difficult to read, and with no distinction between calendar units (months, years)
 12  // and fixed units (hours, minutes, seconds)
 13  const duréeTrajet = Temporal.Duration.from({ hours: 2, minutes: 45 });
 14  console.log("duréeTrajet =", duréeTrajet.toString());
 15  console.log("heures =", duréeTrajet.hours, ", minutes =", duréeTrajet.minutes);
 16  
 17  // You can also create a duration based on its notation ISO 8601
 18  const duréeChantier = Temporal.Duration.from("P3M2W"); // 3 months and 2 weeks
 19  console.log("duréeChantier =", duréeChantier.toString());
 20  
 21  // total() converts an integer duration into a single unit
 22  console.log("duréeTrajet en minutes =", duréeTrajet.total("minutes"));
 23  
 24  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 25  // 2) Add a duration to a date or time
 26  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 27  const départ = Temporal.PlainTime.from("08:15:00");
 28  const arrivée = départ.add(duréeTrajet);
 29  console.log("départ =", départ.toString(), ", arrivée =", arrivée.toString());
 30  
 31  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 32  // 3) Temporal.Instant: a point PRÉCIS and UNIVERSEL in time
 33  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 34  // unlike PlainDateTime or ZonedDateTime (which involve a calendar
 35  // and time zone), Instant simply represents “a moment,” like a timestamp—
 36  // is the direct replacement for "new Date(quelqueChose).getTime()"
 37  const maintenant = Temporal.Now.instant();
 38  console.log("maintenant (Instant) =", maintenant.toString());
 39  console.log("époque en millisecondes =", maintenant.epochMilliseconds);
 40  
 41  // An Instant can be converted to a ZonedDateTime in any time zone,
 42  // since a specific time corresponds to a different local time depending on the time zone
 43  const maintenantAParis = maintenant.toZonedDateTimeISO("Europe/Paris");
 44  const maintenantASydney = maintenant.toZonedDateTimeISO("Australia/Sydney");
 45  console.log("maintenant à Paris =", maintenantAParis.toString());
 46  console.log("maintenant à Sydney =", maintenantASydney.toString());
 47  
 48  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 49  // 4) Duration between two times, and comparison
 50  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 51  const début = Temporal.Instant.from("2026-08-24T09:00:00Z");
 52  const fin = Temporal.Instant.from("2026-08-24T17:30:00Z");
 53  console.log("durée de la journée de travail =", début.until(fin).toString());
 54  console.log("début avant fin :", Temporal.Instant.compare(début, fin) < 0);
  • A Duration can be constructed from an object ({ hours: 2, minutes: 45 }) or a string in the format ISO 8601 ("P3M2W" for 3 months and 2 weeks);
  • total(unit) converts an entire duration into a single unit (for example, minutes);
  • The same Instant can be converted to ZonedDateTime in any time zone—a specific instant corresponds to a different local time depending on your location.

docs.title: 17.6. [04-comparaison-avec-Date] script
docs.text:
This script addresses, one by one, the historical flaws in Date mentioned in the introduction and shows how Temporal corrects them:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU ECMAScript 2026] Temporal vs. Date: Common Pitfalls Corrected
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  // [nécessite Node 26+ - voir temporal/README.md]
  6  
  7  // [Date] has not been removed from the language (the existing code continues to work),
  8  // but [Temporal] is now the recommended API for all new code.
  9  // This script illustrates, one by one, the historical flaws of [Date].
 10  
 11  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 12  // Pitfall #1: Months numbered from 0 to 11 in Date (January = 0!)
 13  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 14  const dateAoût = new Date(2026, 7, 24); // 7 = August?! Very confusing for a beginner
 15  console.log("[Date] mois affiché =", dateAoût.getMonth(), "(mais c'est bien le mois d'août)");
 16  
 17  const plainDateAoût = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 8, day: 24 });
 18  console.log("[Temporal] mois affiché =", plainDateAoût.month, "(8 = août, comme tout le monde s'y attend)");
 19  
 20  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 21  // Pitfall #2: `Date` is mutable—a shared object can be modified by mistake
 22  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 23  function ajouterUneSemaineDate(date: Date): Date {
 24    date.setDate(date.getDate() + 7); // Modifies the object passed as a parameter!
 25    return date;
 26  }
 27  const dateOriginale = new Date(2026, 7, 24);
 28  const dateAvecUneSemaineEnPlus = ajouterUneSemaineDate(dateOriginale);
 29  // Pitfall: dateOriginale was also modified, even though that wasn’t necessarily intended
 30  console.log("[Date] dateOriginale après l'appel =", dateOriginale.toDateString(), "(modifiée !)");
 31  console.log("[Date] dateAvecUneSemaineEnPlus =", dateAvecUneSemaineEnPlus.toDateString());
 32  
 33  function ajouterUneSemaineTemporal(date: Temporal.PlainDate): Temporal.PlainDate {
 34    return date.add({ days: 7 }); // returns a NOUVEL object; does not modify anything
 35  }
 36  const plainDateOriginale = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 8, day: 24 });
 37  const plainDateAvecUneSemaineEnPlus = ajouterUneSemaineTemporal(plainDateOriginale);
 38  console.log("[Temporal] plainDateOriginale après l'appel =", plainDateOriginale.toString(), "(inchangée)");
 39  console.log("[Temporal] plainDateAvecUneSemaineEnPlus =", plainDateAvecUneSemaineEnPlus.toString());
 40  
 41  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 42  // pitfall #3: Date’s parsing of a string is ambiguous
 43  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 44  // Depending on the string format, "new Date(...)" interprets it sometimes as local time,
 45  // or as UTC—a common pitfall in production
 46  console.log("[Date] new Date('2026-08-24') =", new Date("2026-08-24").toString(), "(interprété en UTC)");
 47  console.log("[Date] new Date('2026-08-24 00:00:00') =", new Date("2026-08-24 00:00:00").toString(), "(interprété en heure locale)");
 48  // -> The two lines above may display different times for the “same” date!
 49  
 50  // With Temporal, the behavior is always explicit and unambiguous:
 51  // A PlainDate has no time at all; a ZonedDateTime requires a specific time zone
 52  console.log("[Temporal] PlainDate.from('2026-08-24') =", Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-08-24").toString());
 53  
 54  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 55  // Pitfall #4: Date cannot natively calculate a “proper” duration
 56  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 57  const date1 = new Date(2026, 0, 1);
 58  const date2 = new Date(2026, 7, 24);
 59  const millisecondesEntreLesDeux = date2.getTime() - date1.getTime();
 60  const joursEntreLesDeux = millisecondesEntreLesDeux / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24);
 61  console.log("[Date] jours entre les deux dates (calcul manuel) =", joursEntreLesDeux);
 62  
 63  const p1 = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 1, day: 1 });
 64  const p2 = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 8, day: 24 });
 65  console.log("[Temporal] durée entre les deux dates =", p1.until(p2).toString());
 66  
 67  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 68  // In summary: Temporal is immutable, unambiguous regarding time zones, and uses
 69  // separate types for each use case (date only, time only, specific moment,
 70  // date+time+time zone...), and reliable arithmetic even around
 71  // daylight saving time changes and months of varying lengths.
 72  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • [piège n°1]: The months in Date are numbered from 0 to 11 (however, new Date(2026, 7, 24) does indeed refer to August)—a common source of confusion for beginners;
  • [piège n°2]: Date is mutable—modifying a Date object passed as a function parameter also modifies the original, which may come as a surprise; Temporal.PlainDate.add() always returns a new object;
  • [piège n°3]: Parsing a string using <span style="color: #9a3412">new Date(...) is ambiguous depending on its exact format (local time or UTC); <span style="color: #9a3412">Temporal is always explicit;
  • [piège n°4]: Date cannot natively calculate a “clean” duration between two dates (you must subtract timestamps in milliseconds and divide manually); Temporal.PlainDate.until(...) does this directly.
Important—transparency regarding verification: the scripts in this chapter require Node.js 26 or later. Since the environment in which this course was prepared was limited to Node.js 22, Claude was unable to run them directly—unlike all the scripts in the previous chapters. Readers (who have confirmed that they work properly on their own machines, using Node.js 26) are invited to run them themselves to see the actual results.

docs.title: 3. The Basics of TypeScript
docs.text:
Note: Hereinafter, the term [TypeScript] will refer to the language as defined by its version 6, a typed superset of ECMAScript 2026.

The scripts in this chapter are located in the [bases] folder of the project.

docs.title: 3.1. [bases-01] script
docs.text:
This script reproduces the introductory example from the original JavaScript course, translated and typed in TypeScript:

  1  /* eslint-disable no-constant-condition */
  2  'use strict';
  3  // this is a comment
  4  // constant
  5  const nom: string = "dupont";
  6  // a screen display
  7  console.log("nom : ", nom);
  8  // an array with elements of different types
  9  // [any] because this array intentionally mixes several types (demonstration)
 10  const tableau: any[] = ["un", "deux", 3, 4];
 11  // its number of elements
 12  let n: any = tableau.length;
 13  // a loop
 14  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
 15    console.log("tableau[", i, "] = ", tableau[i]);
 16  }
 17  // initializing two variables with the contents of an array
 18  let [chaine1, chaine2]: string[] = ["chaine1", "chaine2"];
 19  // concatenation of the two strings
 20  const chaine3 = chaine1 + chaine2;
 21  // displaying the result
 22  console.log([chaine1, chaine2, chaine3]);
 23  // using a function
 24  affiche(chaine1);
 25  // The type of a variable can be known
 26  afficheType("n", n);
 27  afficheType("chaine1", chaine1);
 28  afficheType("tableau", tableau);
 29  // A variable's type can change during execution
 30  // [n] is typed as [any] above: this is precisely what allows TypeScript
 31  // to accept this reassignment along the way, as in JavaScript
 32  n = "a changé";
 33  afficheType("n", n);
 34  // a function can return a result
 35  let res1: any = f1(4);
 36  console.log("res1=", res1);
 37  // a function can return an array of values
 38  let res2: any, res3: any;
 39  [res1, res2, res3] = f2();
 40  console.log("(res1,res2,res3)=", [res1, res2, res3]);
 41  // we could have retrieved these values into an array
 42  let t: any[] = f2();
 43  for (let i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
 44    console.log("t[", i, "]=", t[i]);
 45  }
 46  // tests
 47  for (let i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
 48    // displays only strings
 49    if (typeof (t[i]) === "string") {
 50      console.log("t[", i, "]=", t[i]);
 51    }
 52  }
 53  // comparison operators == and ===
 54  if ("2" == (2 as any)) {
 55    console.log("avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2");
 56  } else {
 57    console.log("avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2");
 58  }
 59  if (("2" as any) === 2) {
 60    console.log("avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2");
 61  } else {
 62    console.log("avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2");
 63  }
 64  // more tests
 65  for (let i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
 66    // displays only integers greater than 10
 67    if (typeof (t[i]) === "number" && Math.floor(t[i]) === t[i] && t[i] > 10) {
 68      console.log("t[", i, "]=", t[i]);
 69    }
 70  }
 71  // a while loop
 72  t = [8, 5, 0, -2, 3, 4];
 73  let i = 0;
 74  let somme = 0;
 75  while (i < t.length && t[i] > 0) {
 76    console.log("t[", i, "]=", t[i]);
 77    somme += t[i];
 78    i++;
 79  }
 80  console.log("somme=", somme);
 81  
 82  // the program stops because there is no more executable code
 83  
 84  //displays
 85  //----------------------------------
 86  function affiche(chaine: string): void {
 87    // displays a string
 88    console.log("chaine=", chaine);
 89  }
 90  
 91  //afficheType
 92  //----------------------------------
 93  function afficheType(name: string, variable: unknown): void {
 94    // displays the variable type
 95    console.log("type[variable ", name, "]=", typeof (variable));
 96  }
 97  
 98  //----------------------------------
 99  function f1(param: number): number {
100    // adds 10 to the parameter
101    return param + 10;
102  }
103  
104  //----------------------------------
105  function f2(): any[] {
106    // returns 3 values
107    return ["un", 0, 100];
108  }

Let's comment on this code:

  • line 5: [const nom: string = "dupont"] — in TypeScript, you can explicitly annotate a variable’s type by adding type after its name. Here, name is guaranteed to be a string throughout the program;
  • line 10: [const array: any[] = ...] — this array intentionally mixes strings and numbers. The type any[] tells TypeScript not to check the types of the elements: this is an explicit choice, distinct from an omission of typing (which strict mode prohibits);
  • line 12: [let n: any = tableau.length] — n is typed as any because, later on (line 28), it is reassigned a string after having been assigned a number. In JavaScript, a variable can change types freely; in TypeScript, this is permitted only if explicitly allowed with any</span> (or a type union, such as <span style="color: #9a3412">number | string</span>);
  • line 51: ["2" == (2 as any)] — TypeScript prohibits, by default, comparing two values of incompatible types (string and number) using ==. The expression (2 as any) is a type assertion: we explicitly tell TypeScript “treat this value as any; do not check its type here,” which deliberately illustrates the type coercion specific to the == operator;
  • lines 82–84: the function [function afficheType(name: string, variable: unknown): void] types its second parameter as unknown rather than any. Unlike any</span>, unknown prohibits using the value without first checking it—here, we simply use <span style="color: #9a3412">typeof(variable), which is allowed even on unknown;
  • lines 89–92: Functions now have an explicit return type (: number, : void..., etc.), written after the parameter list.

    • Let’s run this script:

    npx tsx bases/bases-01.ts

    Execution result:

      1  nom :  dupont
  2  tableau[ 0 ] =  un
  3  tableau[ 1 ] =  deux
  4  tableau[ 2 ] =  3
  5  tableau[ 3 ] =  4
  6  [ 'chaine1', 'chaine2', 'chaine1chaine2' ]
  7  chaine= chaine1
  8  type[variable  n ]= number
  9  type[variable  chaine1 ]= string
 10  type[variable  tableau ]= object
 11  type[variable  n ]= string
 12  res1= 14
 13  (res1,res2,res3)= [ 'un', 0, 100 ]
 14  t[ 0 ]= un
 15  t[ 1 ]= 0
 16  t[ 2 ]= 100
 17  t[ 0 ]= un
 18  avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2
 19  avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2
 20  t[ 2 ]= 100
 21  t[ 0 ]= 8
 22  t[ 1 ]= 5
 23  somme= 13

docs.title: 3.2. script [bases-02]
docs.text:
The [bases-02] script demonstrates the use of the keywords [let] and [const]:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // To initialize a variable, use `let` or `const`
  3  // `let` for variables
  4  let x: number = 4;
  5  x++;
  6  console.log(x);
  7  // `const` for constants
  8  const y: number = 10;
  9  x += y;
 10  // is not allowed
 11  y++;
  • [let] declares a variable whose value can change (lines 4–5);
  • [const] declares a constant whose value cannot change (line 8);
  • line 11: an attempt is made to reassign the constant y using y++. This is where TypeScript offers a real advantage over JavaScript.

Even before executing the script, the type check flags the error:

npx tsc --noEmit

Execution result:

  1  bases/bases-02.ts(11,1): error TS2588: Cannot assign to 'y' because it is a constant.

In the standard JavaScript version, this same error would not have been detected until runtime. Let’s run this script anyway using tsx (which executes the code without first performing type checking, unlike tsc) to see the error as JavaScript actually raises it:

npx tsx bases/bases-02.ts

Execution result:

  1  5
  2  TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
  3      at bases/bases-02.ts:11:1
Important: tsx transpiles TypeScript into JavaScript without type checking (as Babel does), for fast execution during development. This is why this script runs (and crashes during execution) even though it does not compile with tsc. To be notified of the error before execution, use VSCode (which runs tsc in the background) or the `npm run check` command.

docs.title: 3.3. script [bases-03]
docs.text:
Illustrates the scope of global variables, which are visible inside a function:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // Variable scope
  3  let count: number = 1;
  4  function doSomething(): void {
  5    // `count` is known here
  6    console.log("count=", count);
  7  }
  8  // call
  9  doSomething();

npx tsx bases/bases-03.ts

Execution result:

  1  count= 1

docs.title: 3.4. script [bases-04]
docs.text:
A local variable within a function hides (masks) a global variable with the same name:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // variable scope
  3  const count: number = 1;
  4  function doSomething(): void {
  5    // the local variable masks the global variable
  6    const count = 2;
  7    console.log("count inside function=", count);
  8  }
  9  // global variable
 10  console.log("count outside function=", count);
 11  // local variable
 12  doSomething();

npx tsx bases/bases-04.ts

Execution result:

  1  count outside function= 1
  2  count inside function= 2

docs.title: 3.5. script [bases-05]
docs.text:
A local variable (const count inside the function) is not visible outside that function:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // variable scope
  3  function doSomething(): void {
  4    // local variable within the function
  5    const count = 2;
  6    console.log("count inside function=", count);
  7  }
  8  // Here, `count` is not defined
  9  console.log("count outside function=", count);
 10  doSomething();

Here again, TypeScript detects the problem during compilation—no need to run the script to find out:

npx tsc --noEmit

Execution result:

  1  bases/bases-05.ts(9,40): error TS2304: Cannot find name 'count'.

And when run with tsx:

npx tsx bases/bases-05.ts

Execution result:

  1  ReferenceError: count is not defined
  2      at bases/bases-05.ts:9:40

docs.title: 3.6. script [bases-06]
docs.text:
This script compares the block scope ([let], [const]) to the absence of block scope ([var]):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // The keyword [let] is used to define a block-scope variable
  3  {
  4    // The variable [count] is known only within this block
  5    let count: number = 1;
  6    console.log("count=", count);
  7  }
  8  // Here, the variable [count] is not recognized
  9  count++;
 10  
 11  // The keyword [const] is used to define a block-scope variable
 12  {
 13    // The variable [count2] is known only within this block
 14    const count2: number = 1;
 15    console.log("count=", count2);
 16  }
 17  // Here, the variable [count2] is not recognized
 18  count2++;
 19  
 20  // The keyword [var] cannot be used to define a block-scope variable
 21  {
 22    // The variable [count3] will be globally known
 23    var count3: number = 1;
 24    console.log("count=", count3);
 25  }
 26  // Here, the variable [count3] is known
 27  count3++;
  • A variable declared with [let] or [const] inside a { } block exists only within that block;
  • a variable declared with [var] ignores blocks: it remains visible throughout the entire function (or script) that contains it—this was the only behavior available prior to ECMAScript in 2015, which was the source of many bugs, hence the recommendation to always prefer [let]/[const].

Compilation:

docs.title: 3.9. script [bases-09]
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] This script features operators that appeared in ECMAScript 2020–2021 and are now very commonly used:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] some modern operators that are widely used on a daily basis
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7  // 1) the null coalescing operator [??]  (ECMAScript 2020)
  8  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  9  // with [||], a "false" value (0, "", false, NaN, ...) triggers the default value,
 10  //, which isn’t always what we want
 11  const quantité1: number = 0;
 12  console.log("avec ||  : quantité1 || 10 =", quantité1 || 10); // -> 10 (bug! 0 is actually a valid quantity)
 13  // [??] only triggers the default value if the value is null or undefined
 14  console.log("avec ??  : quantité1 ?? 10 =", quantité1 ?? 10); // -> 0 (correct)
 15  
 16  const quantité2: number | null = null;
 17  console.log("quantité2 ?? 10 =", quantité2 ?? 10); // -> 10 (quantity2 is null)
 18  const quantité3: number | undefined = undefined;
 19  console.log("quantité3 ?? 10 =", quantité3 ?? 10); // -> 10 (quantity3 is undefined)
 20  
 21  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 22  // 2) Optional chaining [?.]  (ECMAScript 2020)
 23  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 24  // Before 2020, to safely access a deep property, you had to
 25  // test each level: if (person && personne.adresse && personne.adresse.ville) ...
 26  
 27  // common interface: [adresse] is optional (person2 doesn't have one)
 28  interface PersonneAvecAdresseOptionnelle {
 29    nom: string;
 30    adresse?: { ville: string };
 31  }
 32  
 33  const personne1: PersonneAvecAdresseOptionnelle = {
 34    nom: "Dupont",
 35    adresse: {
 36      ville: "Nantes"
 37    }
 38  };
 39  const personne2: PersonneAvecAdresseOptionnelle = {
 40    nom: "Martin"
 41    // no address!
 42  };
 43  
 44  // [?.] stops evaluation and returns [undefined] as soon as a step is null or undefined
 45  // instead of throwing a "Cannot read properties of undefined" error
 46  console.log("personne1 ville =", personne1.adresse?.ville);
 47  console.log("personne2 ville =", personne2.adresse?.ville); // -> undefined, no error
 48  
 49  // You can combine [?.] and [??] to provide a replacement value
 50  console.log("personne2 ville (avec défaut) =", personne2.adresse?.ville ?? "ville inconnue");
 51  
 52  // [?.] also works on method calls...
 53  interface ObjetAvecMéthode {
 54    direBonjour(): string;
 55    direAurevoir?(): string;
 56  }
 57  const objetAvecMéthode: ObjetAvecMéthode = {
 58    direBonjour() {
 59      return "bonjour !";
 60    }
 61  };
 62  console.log("appel méthode existante :", objetAvecMéthode.direBonjour?.());
 63  console.log("appel méthode absente   :", objetAvecMéthode.direAurevoir?.()); // -> undefined, no error
 64  
 65  // ...and when accessing an array element
 66  const tableauOuNull: number[] | null = null;
 67  console.log("élément d'un tableau absent :", tableauOuNull?.[0]); // -> undefined
 68  
 69  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 70  // 3) logical assignment operators [||=], [&&=], [??=]  (ECMAScript 2021)
 71  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 72  // These operators combine a logical test and an assignment into a single statement
 73  
 74  // [a ??= b] is equivalent to [a = a ?? b]: assigns b only if a is null/undefined
 75  interface Configuration {
 76    délai: number;
 77    page?: number;
 78  }
 79  const config: Configuration = { délai: 0, page: undefined };
 80  config.délai ??= 1000; // The delay is already 0 (valid value) -> remains unchanged
 81  config.page ??= 1;     // page is undefined -> becomes 1
 82  console.log("config après ??= :", config);
 83  
 84  // [a ||= b] is equivalent to [a = a || b]: affects b if a is "false" (0, "", null, undefined, false...)
 85  let messageAffiché: string = "";
 86  messageAffiché ||= "message par défaut";
 87  console.log("messageAffiché après ||= :", messageAffiché);
 88  
 89  // [a &&= b] is equivalent to [a = a && b]: assigns a value to b only if a is already "true"
 90  interface UtilisateurConnecté {
 91    nom: string;
 92    connecté?: boolean;
 93  }
 94  let utilisateurConnecté: UtilisateurConnecté | null = { nom: "Ana" };
 95  utilisateurConnecté &&= { ...utilisateurConnecté, connecté: true };
 96  console.log("utilisateurConnecté après &&= :", utilisateurConnecté);
 97  
 98  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 99  // 4) Numeric separators [_]  (ECMAScript 2021)
100  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
101  // purely visual: makes large numbers more readable in the source code
102  const unMillion: number = 1_000_000;
103  const carteBancaire: bigint = 1234_5678_9012_3456n; // combined here with a BigInt (see below)
104  console.log("unMillion =", unMillion);
105  console.log("carteBancaire =", carteBancaire);
106  
107  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
108  // 5) the [BigInt] type  (ECMAScript 2020)
109  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
110  // the [number] type of JavaScript loses precision beyond approximately 2^53
111  console.log("Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER =", Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER);
112  console.log("Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 =", Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1);
113  console.log("Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 =", Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2); // -> same result as +1, imprecise!
114  
115  // A [BigInt] is written with a final [n], or is constructed using BigInt(...)
116  const grandNombre1: bigint = 9007199254740993n;
117  const grandNombre2: bigint = BigInt("9007199254740993");
118  console.log("grandNombre1 =", grandNombre1, ", type =", typeof (grandNombre1));
119  console.log("grandNombre1 === grandNombre2 :", grandNombre1 === grandNombre2);
120  // A BigInt and a number cannot be directly combined in a calculation
121  try {
122    console.log((grandNombre1 as any) + 1); // causes an error: [TypeError]
123  } catch (error: any) {
124    console.log("erreur attendue :", error.message);
125  }
126  // You must convert explicitly
127  console.log("grandNombre1 + 1n =", grandNombre1 + 1n);

Let’s discuss the most important new features:

  • [??], null coalescing (ECMAScript 2020): Unlike [||], which triggers its default value for any “false” value (0, "", false...), [??] is triggered only if the value is null or undefined. This is the right choice for a quantity that can legitimately be 0;
  • [?.], optional chaining (ECMAScript 2020): stops evaluation and returns undefined as soon as an intermediate step is null or undefined</span>, instead of throwing an error. Also works on method calls (objet.méthode?.()) and on indexing (array?.[0]);
  • [||=], [&&=], [??=], logical assignment operators (ECMAScript 2021): combine a logical test and an assignment into a single expression (a ??= b is equivalent to a = a ?? b);
  • the numeric separators 1_000_000 (ECMAScript 2021): purely visual, they make large numbers more readable in the source code;
  • the type [BigInt] (ECMAScript 2020), denoted with a final “n” (9007199254740993n): unlike <span style="color: #9a3412">number</span>, it does not lose precision beyond <span style="color: #9a3412">Number.MAX\_SAFE\_INTEGER</span>. A <span style="color: #9a3412">BigInt</span> and a <span style="color: #9a3412">number cannot be mixed directly in a calculation, as shown by the script’s try/catch block.
    • npx tsx bases/bases-09.ts

    Execution result:

      1  avec ||  : quantité1 || 10 = 10
  2  avec ??  : quantité1 ?? 10 = 0
  3  quantité2 ?? 10 = 10
  4  quantité3 ?? 10 = 10
  5  personne1 ville = Nantes
  6  personne2 ville = undefined
  7  personne2 ville (avec défaut) = ville inconnue
  8  appel méthode existante : bonjour !
  9  appel méthode absente   : undefined
 10  élément d'un tableau absent : undefined
 11  config après ??= : { 'délai': 0, page: 1 }
 12  messageAffiché après ||= : message par défaut
 13  utilisateurConnecté après &&= : { nom: 'Ana', 'connecté': true }
 14  unMillion = 1000000
 15  carteBancaire = 1234567890123456n

 17  Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 = 9007199254740992
 18  Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 = 9007199254740992

docs.title: 13. The classes
docs.text:
Here we introduce the classes ECMAScript, typed as TypeScript. Before presenting them, let’s recall (script class-00, previously covered in the chapter “Functions” under the name func-04) that functions can already behave like classes—it is this historical mechanism that the keyword [class] simplifies.

The scripts for this chapter are located in the [classes] folder of the project.

docs.text:
Reminder of the historical mechanism (functions used as classes):

  1  'use strict';
  2  // A function can be used as an object
  3  
  4  // an empty shell
  5  // [any]: The type of [this] is intentionally flexible here, because we assign
  6  // properties to the function itself, APRÈS, in its definition (see below) -
  7  // a pattern that TypeScript cannot deduce on its own
  8  function f(this: any): void {
  9  
 10  }
 11  // to which properties are assigned from the outside
 12  (f as any).prop1 = "val1";
 13  (f as any).show = function (this: any) {
 14    console.log(this.prop1);
 15  };
 16  // use of f
 17  (f as any).show();
 18  
 19  // a function g that behaves like a class
 20  function g(this: any): void {
 21    this.prop2 = "val2";
 22    this.show = function (this: any) {
 23      console.log(this.prop2);
 24    };
 25  }

 27  new (g as any)().show();

docs.title: 13.2. script [class-01]
docs.text:
This script defines a class [Personne], with a constructor, getters/setters, and a method toString:

  2  class Personne {
  3

  5    private _prénom!: string;
  6    private _âge!: number;
  7  
  8    // constructor
  9    constructor(nom: string, prénom: string, âge: number) {
 10      this.nom = nom;
 11      this.prénom = prénom;
 12      this.âge = âge;
 13    }
 14  
 15    // getters and setters
 16    get nom(): string {
 17      return this._nom;
 18    }
 19    set nom(value: string) {
 20      this._nom = value;
 21    }
 22  
 23    get prénom(): string {
 24      return this._prénom;
 25    }
 26    set prénom(value: string) {
 27      this._prénom = value;
 28    }
 29  
 30    get âge(): number {
 31      return this._âge;
 32    }
 33    set âge(value: number) {
 34      this._âge = value;
 35    }
 36  
 37    // toString to JSON
 38    toString(): string {

 40    }
 41  }
 42

 46    console.log("personne=", personne.toString(), typeof (personne), personne instanceof (Personne));

docs.title: 13.5. script [class-04] — polymorphism
docs.text:
This script demonstrates polymorphism in action: where a function expects a parameter of type Person, we can pass a derived type such as Teacher, since it possesses all the attributes of Person. First, we isolate Teacher in its own module, Enseignant.ts:

  1  // imports
  2  // [mise à jour 2026] with Node.js's native ESM; the .js extension is required
  3  // in relative paths (it was optional with the [esm] loader used in 2019)
  4  import Personne from './Personne.js';
  5  
  6  // class
  7  class Enseignant extends Personne {
  8  
  9    // private property (accessed via the getter/setter below)
 10    private _discipline!: string;
 11  
 12    // constructor
 13    constructor(nom: string, prénom: string, âge: number, discipline: string) {
 14      super(nom, prénom, âge);
 15      this.discipline = discipline;
 16    }
 17  
 18    // getters and setters
 19    get discipline(): string {
 20      return this._discipline;
 21    }
 22    set discipline(value: string) {
 23      this._discipline = value;
 24    }
 25  
 26  }
 27  
 28  // export class
 29  export default Enseignant;

The script [class-04] uses this type polymorphically:

  1  // imports
  2  // [mise à jour 2026] with Node.js’s native ESM; the .js extension is required
  3  // in relative paths (it was optional with the [esm] loader used in 2019)
  4  import Enseignant from './Enseignant.js';
  5  import Personne from './Personne.js';
  6  
  7  // function that accepts a person as a parameter
  8  function show(personne: Personne): void {
  9    // in all cases
 10    console.log("paramètre=", personne.toString(), typeof (personne));
 11    // an instance of Person
 12    if (personne instanceof Personne) {
 13      console.log("personne=", personne.toString());
 14    }
 15    // instance of Teacher
 16    if (personne instanceof Enseignant) {
 17      console.log("enseignant=", personne.toString());
 18    }
 19  }
 20  
 21  // call to `show` with a Teacher
 22  show(new Enseignant("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "détective"));
 23  show(new Personne("Marple", "Miss", 70));
  • line 6: function show(person: Person): void — the function expects a parameter of type Person, but accepts any derived type (Teacher) — this is the principle of substitution, which is fundamental to object-oriented programming;
  • Lines 10–16: instanceof allows the behavior to be adapted to the actual type of the received object, beyond its declared type.

docs.title: 13.6. [class-05] script — native private fields
docs.text:
[NOUVEAU depuis 2019] The previous scripts use the TypeScript private modifier (_nom, _prénom...), a protection mechanism that exists only at compile time—at runtime, in pure JavaScript, these fields remain simply normal properties. Since ECMAScript 2022, there have been true private fields, prefixed with #, which are invisible and inaccessible even at runtime:

  1  'use strict';
  2  // ========================================================================
  3  // [NOUVEAU depuis 2019] private fields and static blocks  (ECMAScript 2022)
  4  // ========================================================================
  5  
  6  // In class-01.js, encapsulation was simulated by convention: a property
  7  // named [_nom] (with an underscore) that was accessed via a getter/setter [nom].
  8  // MAIS—nothing really prevented you from writing personne._nom = "xyz" from the outside!
  9  // Since ECMAScript 2022, you can declare VRAIS private fields with a [#]
 10  // prefixed to their names: they are accessible only from within the class.
 11  
 12  class CompteBancaire {
 13  
 14    // private field: exists and is visible only within the methods of this class
 15    #balance: number;
 16  
 17    // private field with a default value
 18    #history: string[] = [];
 19  
 20    // normal public field (no #): accessible from outside, as before
 21    titulaire: string;
 22  
 23    constructor(titulaire: string, soldeInitial: number = 0) {
 24      this.titulaire = titulaire;
 25      this.#balance = soldeInitial;
 26    }
 27  
 28    // public method that provides controlled access to the private field
 29    get solde(): number {
 30      return this.#balance;
 31    }
 32  
 33    déposer(montant: number): void {
 34      this.#balance += amount;
 35      // #ajouterHistorique is a private method, callable only from here
 36      this.#ajouterHistorique(`deposit of ${amount}`);
 37    }
 38  
 39    retirer(montant: number): void {
 40      if (montant > this.#balance) {
 41        throw new Error("solde insuffisant");
 42      }
 43      this.#balance -= amount;
 44      this.#ajouterHistorique(`withdrawal of ${amount}`);
 45    }
 46  
 47    // private method: [#] also works on methods
 48    #ajouterHistorique(operation: string): void {
 49      this.#historique.push(operation);
 50    }
 51  
 52    afficherHistorique(): void {
 53      console.log(`historique de ${this.titulaire} :`, this.#history);
 54    }
 55  }
 56  
 57  // normal use
 58  const compte = new CompteBancaire("Dupont", 100);
 59  compte.déposer(50);
 60  compte.retirer(30);
 61  console.log("solde =", compte.solde); // via the public getter
 62  compte.afficherHistorique();
 63  
 64  // The private field cannot be accessed directly from outside
 65  console.log("compte.#solde direct : impossible, provoque une erreur de syntaxe si on essaie");
 66  // console.log(account.#balance); // Uncommenting this line causes a compilation error TypeScript
 67  
 68  // It also cannot be read using the notation [ ] as with a normal property
 69  console.log("compte['#solde'] =", (compte as any)["#solde"]); // -> undefined; it’s not the same thing
 70  
 71  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 72  // Private fields and methods STATIQUES also exist
 73  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 74  class GénérateurIdentifiant {
 75    // private static field: shared by all instances, invisible from the outside
 76    static #dernierId: number = 0;
 77  
 78    // static initialization block: executed only once, when the class is loaded
 79    // useful for complex initialization that a simple "= value" cannot handle
 80    static {
 81      console.log("[bloc statique] initialisation de GénérateurIdentifiant");
 82      GénérateurIdentifiant.#dernierId = 1000; // custom initial value
 83    }
 84  
 85    // public static method providing controlled access to the private static field
 86    static prochainId(): number {
 87      GénérateurIdentifiant.#dernierId++;
 88      return GénérateurIdentifiant.#dernierId;
 89    }
 90  }
 91  
 92  console.log("prochainId() =", GénérateurIdentifiant.prochainId());
 93  console.log("prochainId() =", GénérateurIdentifiant.prochainId());
 94  console.log("prochainId() =", GénérateurIdentifiant.prochainId());
  • [#solde], [#historique]: true private fields—unlike _nom in the class-01 script, they cannot be accessed from outside the class, even via compte['#solde'] (line 60), which returns undefined rather than the actual value;
  • [#ajouterHistorique]: a private method, callable only from within the class;
  • [static { ... }]: a static initialization block (ES2022), executed only once when the class is loaded—useful for initialization that is more complex than a simple assignment;
  • [static #dernierId]: a private static field, shared by all instances but invisible from the outside.
